summary.scope: All manifest species photo metadata, local file presence, image decode, exact and possible visual duplicate detection; NO expert botanical pixel-ID certification.
summary.inference_caveat: An absent role label is not proof an organ is absent. A matching role label is NOT pixel verification. Perceptual hashes only suggest lookalikes for human review. Image decoding does not verify exact species identification.

rows.parts_to_recheck: LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect the central staminal column in the dark-centered five-petaled flower; then confirm the deeply lobed hairy leaves and long ridged upright pod.

Texas sweet Indian mallow: small yellow 5-petal mallow flower, small hairy heart-based leaves, and a compact dry fruit with about 6–9(–10) unspined mericarps. For A. incanum lookalike count 6–9 style branches instead of 5. DO NOT require a hairless staminal tube: FNA and UT/Kew disagree.

Nonlocal A. incanum comparison: 5 style/stigma branches and about 5 mature fruit segments, often dark-centered reflexed corolla. FNA does not place the species in Texas; a Hays identification merits comparison with A. fruticosum. Do not rely on staminal-column hair alone; A. fruticosum floras disagree.

Go straight to the giant velvety leaves and mature fruit. Velvetleaf has a large ~15 × 20 mm schizocarp forming a conspicuous crown of mericarps with 3–6 mm divergent spines; the style is 13–15-branched.

Treat this as a reproductive-structure plant, not a leaf-shape plant. Look for an annual Acalypha with alternate serrate leaves and separate staminate/pistillate spike portions, then confirm pistillate bracts and the 3-lobed capsule.
Terminal bisexual spike with pistillate flowers below and staminate section above; long multifid styles make the lower spike conspicuous.
Confirm the perennial dioecious habit, rounded to kidney-shaped deeply crenate leaves, and crowded deeply lobed pistillate bracts with multifid styles.

Check opposite SIMPLE palmate leaves, then compare sinus depth and leaf undersides: broad 3–5 lobes with relatively shallow notches are typical; short hairs may occur below. Confirm with paired samaras, buds and bark when available. Do not identify from fall color or canyon habitat alone.

Start with the opposite compound leaves: boxelder is a maple that often looks like an ash. Then confirm the paired V-shaped samaras. In season, note that the tree is dioecious and the small flowers lack petals.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Opposite SIMPLE leaves with one blade deeply palmately divided into usually 5–7 pointed, finely toothed lobes; verify opposite buds and paired winged samaras. Cultivars vary widely in leaf shape and color; red foliage alone is not diagnostic.

Find an opposite SIMPLE leaf with very deep, sharp, angular/V-shaped sinuses and a conspicuously pale to silvery lower face. Check multiple mature leaves, not a single atypical blade; confirm opposite twig nodes and paired samaras when present.

Look at a fully developed stem leaf first: narrow outline but very finely divided into many tiny fernlike segments (usually 1–2-pinnately dissected). Then inspect the flat-topped cluster of numerous tiny composite heads. Check a single head from the side for several rows of overlapping phyllaries; do not infer native status or identity fr

Find an OPEN flower and measure the entire slender perianth tube from its base to the expanded limb: about 7–17 cm long and only 1–2 mm wide. Compare A. obtusa, whose open perianth is much shorter (about 2.5–5.5 cm total). Confirm narrow wedge-based opposite leaves and the thin ridges of a mature anthocarp; closed self-pollinating flowers

Measure an intact OPEN flower: perianth about 2.5–5.5 cm total, far shorter than the 7–17 cm tube of A. longiflora. Check broadly triangular or delta-ovate leaves with usually truncate, rounded or somewhat heart-shaped bases; confirm ripe anthocarp ribs and small summit knobs. Tiny closed flowers are not comparable to fully open flowers.

Follow a trailing stem to a node: opposite petiolate, toothed leaves and stems that can root at the nodes. Then inspect a long-stalked solitary head: the disk becomes a conspicuous elongated conical receptacle with chaffy paleae as fruits mature. Confirm with mature compressed dark cypselae; ray color alone is weak.
Inspect the basal rosette: deeply pinnately lobed and spinulose-toothed leaves, then the leafless scape bearing 1–3 heads with 25–53 disk florets.

Inspect alternate cauline toothed leaves on tall branched stems, then a rayless head with 8–12 florets and blunt to shortly acute phyllaries. Unlike A. runcinata, the leaves are not a deeply lobed basal rosette.

Start with the glossy black wiry rachis and delicate fan-shaped pinnules. Southern maidenhair grows from moist limestone seeps, springs, and shaded cliffs, with sori tucked beneath reflexed flap-like false indusia along the pinnule margins.

Look at the overall frond architecture: pinnae spread in a broad, fanlike or horseshoe arrangement from the upper end of a slender dark stipe. Contrast this with the elongated, repeatedly branching triangular fronds of the locally relevant Adiantum capillus-veneris; do not identify by black stalk alone.

Start with a mature capsule: the leathery surface is usually short-prickly or warty. On a flower, check whether stamens project conspicuously beyond petals (about twice petal length). Opposite palmately compound leaves establish buckeye, but do not separate Aesculus species.

Start with the smooth leathery mature capsule and flower structure: stamens are usually included or barely extend beyond the tubular petals. Opposite palmately compound leaves confirm buckeye but not species; yellow-flowered var. flavescens means red color is not a universal species key.

FIRST measure the pedicel from its junction on the flowering branch to the calyx, using multiple flowers. Pedicels can be conspicuously long (reported to about 30 mm). Next compare the calyx lobes, which are very short relative to the tube. Do not decide from purple flower color or right-angle branching.

FIRST measure the flower pedicel from its base to the calyx on several blooms: typically very short, about 1.6–3.2 mm in regional accounts. Inspect the calyx side-on for conspicuous lobes, and check lower leaves for occasional three-parted blades. Do not identify by purple flowers or branch angle.

Start with the broad, fleshy, toothed leaves and terminal spine. Compare mature leaf width and the flowering architecture: a branched panicle supports A. americana, while lechuguilla has narrower leaves and a largely spike-like flowering axis.

Look at narrow rigid rosette leaves, their spaced marginal teeth, and the terminal spine; then inspect the largely spike-like flowering axis. Distinguish A. univittata with leaf-edge detail, not size alone.
Look for opposite long-petioled broad leaves with coarse teeth and three strong basal veins, topped by loose white flat-topped clusters of tiny all-disk heads—no ray florets.

Look for a many-branched, persistent-leaved (evergreen) woody shrub with opposite, serrate, typically 3–5 cm leaves on short 3–10 mm petioles and white to faintly pinkish rayless heads. A. altissima has herbaceous stems and smoother/glabrous cypselae. Mature A. havanensis cypselae are HISPID (hairy).
LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect the base of leaflets on the large alternate pinnate leaf for coarse gland-tipped teeth; female trees also have hanging clusters of twisted winged fruits.

Look closely at one apparent windmill: three separate asymmetric flowers open together within three involucral bracts. Then inspect a mature winged anthocarp and its glands to separate Allionia incarnata from A. choisyi.
Inspect the intact umbel spathe: usually 3–4 bracts with 3–7 veins each. Check flowers versus aerial bulbils; their absence does not exclude this variable species.
Inspect the intact papery spathe: normally 2–3 bracts, about one vein each. The umbel usually bears 10–25 flowers; bulbils are rare.
Look for felted, softly hairy leaves, the five-petaled mallow flower and mallow-style staminal column; compare mericarp fruits.
Measure several mature leaves and compare intact axillary racemes. Leaves often 10–20 × 5–8 mm; short racemes have crowded flower bases. Do not identify by white flowers or scent alone.

Find a mature opposite leaf and an intact axillary flowering raceme. Measure 5–10 fully expanded leaves (often 4–9 × 1.5–6 cm) and inspect the long, loose, often flexuose raceme: individual flower bases are visibly separated. Compare against A. gratissima's generally smaller leaves and short, crowded racemes. Do not rely on fragrance or w
Check prostrate opposite leaves and compact whitish papery flower heads; magnify bracts and compare with A. pungens.
Look at opposite leaves and rounded white flower heads on slender stalks; inspect bracts with a hand lens to distinguish from other Alternanthera.
Inspect opposite leaves, creeping stems and the sharp yellowish bracts on small dense flower heads.
Tall nearly glabrous dioecious amaranth with long-petioled leaves and long terminal spikes; pistillate plants have sharp bracts longer than the tepals.
Small annual amaranth with mostly axillary congested flower clusters rather than a big terminal spike, and relatively small ovate-to-rhombic leaves.
Robust upright pigweed with a reddish lower stem, obvious soft hairs on the upper stem and branches, and a short thick terminal green flower spike.
Low annual with axillary flower clusters from base to top; the cluster axes become thick, inflated and hard at maturity, with uniquely keeled flower bracts.
Bushy upright amaranth with the easiest character in the genus: a pair of sharp spines at nearly every leaf node.
Smooth green annual with slender terminal spikes, rounded or notched leaf tips, only three tepals, and a small indehiscent rugose fruit.

Inspect the yellow head from below: long green outer phyllaries, a domed disk and notched ray tips. Then inspect alternate leaves with clasping upper leaf bases. A mature cypsela has papery pappus scales.

Start at a middle or upper leaf node: the opposite narrow leaves have rounded ear-like (auriculate), often clasping bases. Follow the leaf axil to a loose, stalked cyme with several tiny flowers; inspect the ribbed floral tube, then a mature globose capsule. Compare cluster stalk length and leaf bases with A. coccinea.
Inspect opposite clasping leaves, four-angled stem and small axillary flower clusters. Check the floral tube, calyx appendages and capsule against A. auriculata; color alone is insufficient.
Low gray prairie subshrub with densely silky compound leaves and narrow upright violet-purple flower spikes.

Think tall riparian Amorpha: false indigo bush is a much larger open shrub with long pinnate leaves, many broad oval leaflets, and elongated purple flower spikes carried at the ends of upper branches.

Start with the smooth-looking green compound leaves and upright woody shrub habit. Roemer's false indigo has pinnate leaves with relatively large mostly glabrous leaflets and terminal purple flower racemes that rise above the foliage.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check a simple, heart-shaped to broadly ovate serrated leaf, then the vine's tendril or fruit cluster opposite a leaf. The strongest tie-breaker against Vitis is the cut stem: Ampelopsis has continuous white pith; confirm this rather than relying on berries alone.

LOOK HERE FIRST: find stiff, sharply angled green stems that appear almost leafless; inspect the nodes for clusters of tiny separate male or female flowers. Confirm minute alternate scale-like upper leaves and reddish fringed stipules rather than assuming the green shoots are grass blades.

Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales. Do not identify this species from habit/color alone; compare

Find many small YELLOW RADIATE heads crowded in roughly level or rounded terminal clusters. Confirm with pale whitish phyllaries lacking green nerve borders and longer DISC-floret pappus scales; compare Gutierrezia texana and Amphiachyris amoena before naming.

Inspect flowers SIDE-ON and measure the narrow corolla tube: 6–9(–10) mm. A. longiflora is (20–)28–41(–45) mm. Check sepals (0.8–1.8(–2) mm), leaves and eventual follicles. Do not assign var. texana from species-only records.
View flower SIDE-ON: corolla tube (20–)28–41(–45) mm, much longer than A. ciliata at 6–9(–10) mm. Measure the whole tube with a ruler. A frontal flower view cannot establish tube length.

Start with the fluffy head. Bushy bluestem makes dense broomlike to cottony clusters near the top of the plant, with paired short rames packed inside and emerging from upper leaf sheaths. The inflorescence looks bushy rather than like separate turkey-foot fingers.

Look for narrow silky racemes tucked partly inside flattened spathe-like upper sheaths. Mature plants often turn straw to orange-brown and hold the pale silky seedheads into winter. It does not make the dense brushy crown of bushy bluestem or the digitate turkey foot of big bluestem.
Start at the top: big bluestem usually has 2–6 fingerlike racemes radiating together, often forming the classic turkey-foot. It is a tall robust prairie grass, not a fluffy plume.

Look for a leafless flower stalk with a terminal umbel of funnel-shaped six-tepaled flowers. Look into the throat for the distinctive crown made by joined stamen filaments. Confirm basal linear leaves; do not use flower color alone.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Find the upright, narrow spore-bearing pair of basal pinnae that rises above the broad green sterile part of the frond. These are fertile fern leaf divisions, NOT flowers. Check the straw-colored stalk and once-pinnate blade with 4–7 pairs of mostly lanceolate pinnae.

On a flowering plant, photograph the entire scape: ONE tier of three leaflike involucral bracts sits ABOVE the scape midpoint. Then compare multiple basal leaves to that bract tier: all basal leaves are divided differently from the bracts. Flowers alone are not enough.

Look at the entire flowering scape: ONE tier of three involucral bracts sits BELOW the midpoint. Examine multiple basal leaves: at least one is divided similarly to the involucral bracts. Confirm the bract tier and leaf relationship before using the flower.

Start with the woody shrub habit and long red-orange tubular flowers. Flame acanthus is a many-stemmed deciduous shrub with opposite narrow leaves and terminal clusters of narrow two-lipped hummingbird flowers.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Find the mallow-like flower and, most importantly, a mature flattened disk-shaped fruit (schizocarp). Count the wedge-shaped segments (mericarps) and inspect their projecting points; do not identify this plant from a purple leaf blotch or flower color alone.
Small daisy heads with narrow white to pale ray florets, yellow disk and finely dissected to narrow leaves; inspect head bracts and fruit before separating similar daisies.

LOOK HERE FIRST: follow the low, hairy, branching annual stems to individual terminal daisy heads. Check alternate narrow-to-spatulate leaves and the overlapping, pale-margined phyllaries under a head. For the hard separation from perennial A. riddellii, inspect plant duration/root and mature cypsela hairs with magnification; white rays a

Start with the flower architecture: nodding red-and-yellow flowers have five long backward-pointing nectar spurs, while the leaves are divided into rounded fan-shaped leaflets. In Central Texas, look in shaded limestone canyon bottoms and mesic cliffs.

Start with the bark: mature trunks and limbs shed thin outer layers to expose smooth cream, pink, apricot, orange, or red inner bark. Then confirm evergreen simple leaves, urn-shaped pale flowers, and orange-to-red berry-like fruit.
Do not stop at the white petals. Confirm with glaucous foliage plus bud, sepal-horn, and mature capsule armature because Argemone albiflora subsp. texana can look very similar in flower.
Start with the unusually colored flower: rose, pink, red, lavender, or occasionally pale petals above glaucous prickly foliage. Confirm Argemone with yellow latex plus prickly buds and capsules.

Start with sessile leaves and a 3–8 cm axillary inflorescence. The strongest split from A. simulans is that A. aphoroides inflorescences are unisexual; then confirm with 10 stamens and a relatively large 7–9 mm woolly capsule.

Check the leaf node and raceme before anything else: A. humilis has a real 2–10 mm petiole and a tiny 0.7–0.9 cm axillary raceme. Those two measurements separate it quickly from the two sessile, long-racemed project species.
Start with sessile leaves and a long 3.5–12 cm axillary inflorescence. The key split from A. aphoroides is that A. simulans inflorescences are bisexual, then confirm with only 7–8 stamens.
Single divided umbrella leaf; green hooded spathe and elongated protruding spadix; red berries when mature.

Start with one mature intact spikelet: LOWER and UPPER glumes are normally similar in length (about 18–25 mm without their terminal awns); the lower glume often shows THREE TO SEVEN veins when backlit. Then check that the plant is a wiry, freely branched ANNUAL without a persistent perennial basal crown. The open panicle and long spreadin

Start with one mature intact spikelet: the LOWER glume is usually about half the length of the UPPER glume (roughly 6–8 mm versus 11–15 mm, awns excluded) and normally has ONE vein. Then check the rooted plant for a persistent perennial tuft with many basal rolled leaves and hairs around the collar. Three awns and purple color confirm nei

Look low in grasses and open sandy ground. Swanflower is a tiny erect-to-sprawling perennial with very narrow grasslike leaves and a strange brown-purple curved flower arising near the stem. The showy tube is a petaloid fused calyx/perianth, not a normal petal corolla.

Start low on the plant, near the lowest nodes and leaf litter. The strange brown-purple flower has no ordinary petal whorl: the showy structure is a bent, tubular petaloid calyx/perianth. Then confirm the variable lanceolate-to-cordate leaves and the nearly spherical dry capsule.
Start with broad basal leaves, then inspect the tall stalk and clusters of small pale discoid flower heads rather than looking for showy rays.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Is this a rhizomatous upright herb, rather than a large woody sagebrush shrub? Check the soft silvery or two-toned stem leaves (entire, toothed or lobed), then the many small, inconspicuous flower heads in a narrow to branched cluster. Leaf color alone cannot confirm the species.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check for a persistent woody shrub with many short gray-green wedge-shaped leaves, commonly ending in three short rounded teeth. Confirm gray-brown woody stems and, when present, upright sprays of tiny heads. Three tips alone are not proof: compare the shrub habit and leaf proportions.

Start with cane-like jointed culms from thick rhizomes, broad flat leaves, and the large terminal panicle. Inspect the ligule and mature spikelets to separate it from Phragmites; height alone is not a reliable key.

Inspect mature leaf shape and tip: antelopehorns usually has much narrower lanceolate/linear-lanceolate leaves, narrowly tapering to an acute point. Check dense terminal flower heads, often more rounded than in A. viridis, but do not use head shape alone. Its five corona hoods are present; a projecting horn is not the reliable split from

Check red to scarlet reflexed corolla lobes around bright yellow or orange-yellow corona hoods, then inspect the opposite, relatively smooth narrow leaves. Verify the milky latex and erect, often branched habit. Contrast with native butterfly milkweed, which has alternate hairy leaves and clear/watery sap.
Inspect white-tomentose stems and broad opposite leaves; then large rose-purple umbels and the conspicuously star-like individual flowers, hoods and horns.
Look for tall clonal stems with broad opposite leaves, then dense rounded axillary umbels and individual five-hooded flowers; do not use pink color alone.

Orange umbels alone do not prove butterfly milkweed: check typically alternate, hairy leaves and unusually clear/watery sap; tropical milkweed has opposite (sometimes irregularly grouped) smoother leaves, milky latex and usually red-orange corollas with contrasting yellow corona hoods.

Start with the inflorescence position and flower color. Green comet milkweed has tight greenish flower clusters, often from upper leaf axils, with hoods/corona held compactly; leaves are opposite and relatively broad, and the plant lacks the bright green-white spreading flower look of A. viridis.

Look at a mature leaf first: usually oblong to ovate, relatively broad, with a blunt, rounded or shortly acute tip. Then check the flower: five reddish-purple hoods form the corona, but there is no conspicuous projecting horn. Compare the relatively short corona segments with the much longer pale green corolla lobes; confirm against narro

LOOK HERE FIRST: Follow the glossy black stipe into the black rachis all the way through the narrow once-pinnate blade. Check the many small oblong pinnae, usually with a tiny upper-side basal ear (acroscopic auricle). Turn a fertile pinna over to look for 2–5 pairs of elongated sori.

Texas groundplum variety with thick green fleshy pods near the ground. The important look-alike is A. plattensis: compare ovary/pod HAIRS (groundplum generally glabrous versus hairy plattensis) and groove along each pod SUTURE, not just the pod's size.
Small annual milkvetch with pink-purple flowers and very narrow straight pods that split lengthwise when mature.

An ANNUAL milkvetch with showy bicolored purple-blue and white pea flowers, short appressed hairs and slender curved/flattened pods, not a thick inflated groundplum fruit. Check the banner/wing/keel color pattern, leaflets and fruit cross-section.
Low mat-forming annual with many small leaflets, tiny purplish flowers, and slender pods that curve inward as they dry.
Texas annual milkvetch in the Nuttallianus complex with 4–12 flowers per raceme, relatively broad leaflets, and long narrow glabrous pods.

Platte River milkvetch bears relatively large FLESHY pods that can resemble Berlandier's groundplum. Examine the developing OVARY and pod for fine HAIRS (usually pubescent in plattensis) and two GROOVED pod seams (sutures); the plump fruit alone is not distinctive.
Narrow gray-green scaly leaves on woody branches; seed-bearing bracts with four broad wings.
Look for an open drooping oat panicle bearing individual large spikelets, often with long bent and twisted awns; examine florets and hairy callus.
Recognize a tiny free-floating fern mat of overlapping, scale-like paired leaves, often reddish; check roots beneath the water surface.
Look for a low creeping wetland mat with fleshy, small, sessile oblong-to-obovate leaves and solitary pale blue-white flowers arising from the leaf axils.
Look for leaves divided into two rounded lobes by a central notch, pink-white orchidlike flowers, and flat legume pods.
Treat as a nursery/lookalike comparison: pinnate evergreen leaves with many holly-like leaflets and blue-purple berry clusters. It is not native to Texas under the current Kew concept.

Start with leaf architecture, not just leaflet count. Texas barberry usually has 5–9 leaflets, often with a reduced basal pair close to the rachis base, a dull gray-green reticulate surface, and a more open taller shrub form than agarita.

Start with the leaves: agarita is usually trifoliolate, with 3 stiff holly-like leaflets, blue- to yellow-green foliage, and a dense rounded shrub habit. Yellow spring flowers are followed by red berries.
Check the yellow-rayed flower heads and leafy basal growth, then examine the green disc florets and phyllaries to separate other Berlandiera species.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Examine the flower head from both sides. The yellow ray florets have reddish-maroon veins underneath, and the head is cupped by broad overlapping green involucral bracts (phyllaries). Look for a dark maroon disk and soft, often lyrately lobed gray-green basal leaves. Smell may be chocolate-like, especially in the morning,

Look for a shrub with small crenate leaves that are densely gray-white beneath from stellate hairs. Then confirm dioecious flowers and the 3-lobed capsule; stipule and stamen characters help separate close Bernardia species.

FIRST photograph an ENTIRE middle stem leaf still attached at its OPPOSITE node: B. frondosa is usually compound, each leaf divided into THREE distinct serrated leaflets (sometimes five), each leaflet with its own little stalk; don't count opposite leaves as 'leaflets.' SECOND look under its small orange-yellow DISK HEAD for an outer ring

FIRST find a MIDDLE STEM LEAF still attached to an opposite leaf node: each leaf is SIMPLE (one lance-shaped blade), sessile or nearly so, often toothed, rather than three separate leaflets attached to a common leafstalk (B. frondosa). SECOND inspect head: usually 7–8 showy yellow rays about 15–25 mm long and 5–7+ OUTER CALYCULUS green le
Look at the leaf and climbing organ together: crossvine usually has two broad leaflets, with the third leaflet position modified into a branched tendril ending in adhesive pads.
Opposite toothed leaves on a nettle relative without stinging hairs; tight green flower clusters form slender cylinders along the leaf axils.

LOOK FIRST at a fully mature anthocarp under magnification: conspicuous stalked-glandular hairs and rounded longitudinal ribs favor B. coccinea. Then confirm perennial growth and leaves continuing up the stems; do not key from reddish flower color.

LOOK FIRST at a mature anthocarp: it should be glabrous, with relatively acute five ribs and a truncate to low-conic apex. Then inspect the loose branching flower clusters and whether leaves are mostly on the lower part of an often annual plant.

LOOK FIRST at the mature anthocarp: it is glabrous with five broadly rounded ribs and smooth grooves (sulci). Next inspect the relatively large petaloid perianth (about 4–7 mm) and usually five exserted stamens. Narrow leaves alone are not diagnostic.
Inspect small white-ray daisy heads on finely branched stems; examine narrow leaf blades, disc florets and phyllaries.

Check the stem nodes before the seedhead. Cane bluestem has a conspicuous dense beard/ring of soft hairs around the node, often several millimeters long. Then confirm the fanlike silvery panicle: many primary branches spread nearly as long as the main inflorescence.

Start with the seedhead and nodes. King Ranch bluestem has smooth/glabrous nodes and a loose terminal head of only about 3–8 long fingerlike branches. The stems often kink/change angle at nodes and branch freely from a broad crown. That is very different from silver bluestem's dense cottony mass and cane bluestem's hairy nodes.
Look at the seedhead: a contracted panicle made of many short, densely hairy rames gives the whole inflorescence a silvery-white cottony appearance.
Look at alternate simple leaves and five-lobed funnel-shaped flowers; check the calyx and stamens instead of judging by flower color.
Look at the flowering stem: many short oat-like racemes project and droop from mostly one side of the central axis.

Look at growth form and sex-specific inflorescences before anything else: buffalograss makes a creeping stoloniferous sod; male plants carry small flag-like spikes while female seed clusters are compact, bur-like, and tucked low among the leaves.

Look at the number and shape of the flowering branches: blue grama usually has 1–3 conspicuous unilateral racemes shaped like curved eyebrows or rooster combs, with spikelets packed all the way to the branch tip.

Start with the comb-like branches and the hairy leaf bases. Hairy grama is a tufted perennial with narrow leaves bearing conspicuous papillose-based hairs, usually 1–4 one-sided pectinate branches, and a naked branch tip extending beyond the terminal spikelets.
Look for a much taller, more robust grama than hairy grama, with 3–5 relatively long straight to slightly curved comb-like branches and a naked axis-like projection beyond the spikelets.

Count and inspect the short inflorescence branches near the top: Texas grama usually has about 5–9 tiny, densely hairy/awned lateral branches, often secondarily arranged to one side, instead of the many hanging racemes of sideoats or the 1–3 long combs of blue grama.

Start with the tiny wiry reddish plant and narrow appressed seedhead branches. Red grama is a short perennial bunchgrass with very narrow mostly basal leaves and 2–7 small persistent red to purplish pectinate branches held close to the main axis.
LOOK HERE FIRST: find small greenish axillary umbels beside mostly opposite, shallowly lobed leaves; check for star-branched hairs with a hand lens.

Examine paired nodes and the underside of a mature leaf: leaves often opposite or nearly opposite, densely pale-tomentose beneath and gland-dotted. Confirm on a head by checking layered phyllaries; the outer bracts are at most about half the inner length. Do not identify by stream-gravel habitat alone.

First inspect alternate leaves (often coarsely toothed but occasionally entire) and narrow cylindrical flower heads. Use a loupe to check 18–22 phyllaries in 5–6 overlapping series and 13–20 disk florets. At fruiting, confirm mostly hairless cypselae with 30–35 tawny pappus bristles. Do not use river-gravel habitat or leaf teeth alone.

Start at a mature head and fruit: pappus bristles are plumose to subplumose, with gland-dotted phyllaries. Inspect woody perennial base and leaf nodes, but remember some varieties have alternate rather than opposite leaves. Do not assign a variety from a species-level source row.
Annual brome with a loose nodding branched panicle and elongated awned spikelets; inspect lemma awns and blade/sheath hairs.
Inspect the branching panicle, hairy leaf sheaths, multi-flowered spikelets, awns and lemmas.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Follow the climbing vine to a node and look for a short papery sheath (ocrea) around the stem, a Polygonaceae clue. Check alternate leaves, often with heart-shaped bases. At fruiting, look for drooping clusters of small achenes carried on elongated winged flower stalks; the wing is on the stalk, not the leaf.
Slender herb with opposite narrow leaves and an elongated spike of violet-blue tubular flowers; inspect four-lobed corollas and bracts.
Small woody shrub with opposite leaves and distinct rounded clusters of tiny flowers along an elongated inflorescence; inspect leaf undersides and flower heads.
Annual herb with bristly narrow leaves and small pale five-lobed flowers; inspect the hairy calyx, flower tube and hard nutlets.

Ignore the flower at first and look underwater: submerged leaves are opposite and fan-shaped, split into many fine segments. When flowering, a small white-to-purplish 3-merous flower rises at the surface.

Start with the fruit arrangement and opposite leaves. American beautyberry has tight rings/clusters of vivid purple-magenta berries hugging the stem at the leaf axils, plus opposite serrate leaves on a softly hairy shrub.

Think tall, glaucous perennial with highly dissected fingerlike leaves and NO involucellar bractlets. The inflorescence is paniculate, stipules are usually shed early, and the calyx lobes meet into a pointed bud.

Check growth habit and the structures immediately below the calyx. Winecup is a perennial with low trailing/decumbent stems and an involucel of 3 bractlets beneath the flower. The calyx lobes are already divergent in bud rather than meeting to form a pointed bud.

Start with life form and the underside of the flower. Tall poppymallow is an annual (sometimes biennial) with one to several erect/weakly erect stems and NO involucellar bractlets beneath the calyx. In bud the calyx lobes meet valvately to form a pointed tip.

Look at habit, stipules and inflorescence. Palmleaf poppymallow is an erect-to-weakly-erect perennial with persistent linear-lanceolate stipules, a racemose flower arrangement, no involucellar bractlets, and deeply palmately divided leaves with 3–5 main lobes.
Low trailing plant with opposite ovate toothed leaves and small yellow composite heads from the leaf axils; inspect phyllaries and three-angled fruits.
Strap-like basal foliage and erect raceme of blue-violet six-tepaled flowers with six stamens.
Evergreen tree with shiny three-veined leaves, small pale panicles and dark one-seeded drupes; inspect leaf veins and crushed-leaf odor without relying on scent alone.
Look at the climbing organ first: trumpet creeper clings with short aerial rootlets, then confirm the large opposite odd-pinnate leaves with 7–11 sharply serrated leaflets.
Emergent wetland canna with glaucous narrow leaves and yellow flowers whose showy petal-like parts are mostly staminodes.
Basal rosette of deeply lobed leaves, small four-petaled white flowers and strongly triangular to heart-shaped seedpods.

LOOK HERE FIRST: examine a small white, five-lobed flower arising singly or in a pair from a leaf axil; the leaves are simple with smooth (entire) margins, and a shallow persistent calyx sits at the base of the developing pepper fruit.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Climbing tendrilled vine, divided leaflets and inflated papery three-lobed capsules. Open a mature fruit to see three dark rounded seeds, each with a pale heart-shaped scar.
Woodland Carex with relatively broad, flat green leaves and a loose set of separate spikes: one terminal staminate spike above several pistillate spikes.
Colony-forming woodland sedge with broad leaves and several long drooping pistillate spikes below a raised cluster of staminate spikes.
Tall wetland sedge with broad glaucous leaves and a dense cylindrical inflorescence with long-beaked perigynia.
Small Central Texas canyon sedge with dense tufts, strongly purple-red culm bases, and a few widely separated spikes in dry-mesic calcareous woodland just above streams.
Tall rhizomatous streambank sedge with several long pistillate spikes below 2–3 terminal staminate spikes.
Moist-ground sedge with moderately broad leaves and plump perigynia ending in a short but distinct beak.
Meadow and open-woodland sedge with a somewhat lax oblong inflorescence and unusually long-beaked perigynia with long apical teeth.
Low fine-textured woodland sedge with narrow V-shaped leaves and small separate spikes, especially common on calcareous soils beneath juniper and oak.
Spring-fruiting prairie sedge with 2–4 distinct rounded spikes and large flat silvery-white winged perigynia.
Small fine-textured sedge with very narrow leaves and a compact cluster of several tiny spikes bearing spreading or reflexed perigynia.
Begin with small clustered flower heads and their involucral bracts; inspect leaves and florets under magnification.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Look at the pointed, often spiny leaves and bracts surrounding each terminal flower head. The head is made of many slender tubular florets rather than one flower, on a branching upright plant.
Deciduous tree with pinnate alternate leaves and elongated narrow toothed leaflets; inspect small hickory nuts, husk seams and twigs.
Large deciduous tree with alternate pinnate leaves; elongated sickle-shaped leaflets with toothed margins, ridged husked nuts and compound buds. Inspect leaf rachis and fruit husk.

Start with life cycle and the bracts. Texas paintbrush is an annual, usually with bright red to orange-red showy bracts and a more compact spring-flowering habit than the perennial prairie paintbrushes.

Look at the colored bracts, not just the flowers. Lindheimer's paintbrush is a perennial hemiparasite with narrow leaves, upper leaves often lobed, and a terminal spike whose three-lobed bracts turn orange-red to scarlet around the much less conspicuous tubular flowers.

Start with perennial habit plus bract color and leaf/bract shape. Prairie paintbrush is a perennial of rocky calcareous prairies; bracts can be purple-pink, yellowish, or orange-red depending on form, so color alone is not enough.
Large opposite or whorled heart-shaped leaves, branched clusters of tubular trumpet flowers, and very long slender pod-like capsules.

LOOK HERE FIRST: check the large, heart-shaped, untoothed leaves arranged opposite or in whorls, then inspect upright terminal clusters of large white, purple-and-yellow-marked trumpet flowers; later look for long narrow hanging seed capsules.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Look at a small annual grass with narrow leaves and a relatively stiff, often one-sided, narrow panicle. Examine its crowded, laterally compressed multi-flowered spikelets on short angular branches; verify spikelet florets and a blunt membranous ligule rather than guessing from grass habit.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Alternate toothed leaves with three veins near the base; rounded terminal white flower clusters and three-lobed capsules.
Look for an upright branched woody herb or shrub, alternate simple leaves, and small pale flowers crowded along narrow flowering spikes.
Relatively smooth leaves, strongly asymmetrical leaf base, unarmed tree habit, corky-warty bark.
The white-under-leaf hackberry: dark rough upper leaf surfaces, densely white-tomentose undersides, and light-brown fruit.
Thorny dense shrub habit with small leaves and orange to reddish fruit.
Rough leaf surface plus strongly raised netlike veins beneath; unarmed woody plant.
Grass with dense spiny burr-like groups of florets along a spike; inspect bristle fusion and burr spines, plus hairy ligule.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Inspect the head: outer sterile florets are enlarged and trumpet-like with fringed tips, surrounding shorter central fertile florets. Then turn the head sideways to inspect several rows of non-spiny green phyllaries with dark or pale papery fringed appendages. Check the narrow alternate leaves and slightly woolly stems; b
Inspect a yellow composite flower head surrounded by narrow phyllaries ending in sharp spines; look for winged stem portions.
Check the rounded scalloped leaf blades on long petioles and small clustered flowers close to the ground; inspect where the petiole attaches.

Start with the inflorescence and leaf arrangement. Buttonbush has distinctive spherical white flower heads with projecting styles that look like pincushions, plus opposite or whorled glossy entire leaves on a wet-site shrub.
Look underwater for rootless, branching stems with whorls of stiff, repeatedly forked narrow leaves, especially the bushy shoot tips.
Low spreading perennial with oval leaves and terminal clusters of five-lobed bright blue flowers; inspect tubular calyces and flower bases.
Mexican redbud is the smaller, more xeric-looking redbud: leaves are relatively small, thick, glossy, and characteristically wavy-edged, on a compact multi-trunked tree or large shrub.
Look for the thick glossy leathery leaves. Texas redbud has broad rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with a noticeably shiny upper surface, generally less wavy-edged and larger than Mexican redbud.
Look closely at hairy, often lobed leaves and stems; examine the tiny clustered flowers and their bracts rather than relying on growth habit alone.
Look for finely divided foliage and compound umbels of tiny pale flowers; inspect mature hairy fruits and leaf-sheath bases to separate parsley-family look-alikes.

Start at the base: this is a taprooted ANNUAL, not a rhizomatous perennial. Check flat, herbaceous, non-overlapping leaves; then inspect a mature cypsela with a loupe. The pappus is a minute thickened ring rather than the ~25 obvious bristles of C. ericoides. Compare whole plants with C. effusa and confirm root type before naming.

Find the rhizomatous PERENNIAL base, then inspect the lower stem leaves: oblong to lanceolate-oblong, 6–12 mm wide, with truncate to slightly heart-shaped bases. At fruiting check the pappus, a tiny thickened ring or erose crown <0.1 mm, NOT the conspicuous ~25 bristles of C. ericoides.

Look along the stem first: tiny narrow, densely overlapping, leathery leaves, with a raised midrib and paired longitudinal grooves on the upper face. Confirm the woody/perennial base and, at fruiting, a single series of roughly 24–26 white barbellate pappus bristles; unlike the tiny pappus rings of C. effusa and C. bellidifolia.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Alternate pinnate leaves with many paired narrow leaflets; large unequal yellow petals and dark stamens; narrow flattened legume. Check petiolar nectar gland in a future macro.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Find a low, spreading nightshade-family perennial with deeply wavy or lobed, hairy gray-green leaves. Check its small pale five-lobed flowers and later rounded berries; inspect flower/fruit structures to separate other Chamaesaracha species rather than relying on leaf outline alone.
Look for low growth, small five-lobed pale flowers and berries; inspect calyx and corolla rather than flower color alone.
Examine the low stems, pale five-lobed flowers and calyx; verify species-level characters before separating local Chamaesaracha.
Look for a basal leaf rosette with densely woolly undersides, slender flowering stalks and nodding composite heads; inspect bracts and mature seed pappus.
Broad bamboo-like grass blades and a drooping open inflorescence with distinct flattened oat-like spikelets hanging from slender stalks.
Alternate triangular-to-diamond leaves often dusted with mealy white coating; tiny green flowers crowd into clustered spikes.
Small willow-looking tree with extremely narrow simple leaves, showy trumpet flowers, and very long slender capsules.
Inspect narrow leaves, spiny stems and composite flower heads, including involucral bracts.
Start with the radiating fingerlike terminal grass spikes; examine individual spikelets, their awns and the fertile floret to distinguish related Chloris.

Inspect a mature spikelet under 10–20× first: upper sterile lemma is conspicuously hooded, swollen and nearly round (~1–1.5 mm), often awnless or with 0–1.5 mm awn. Measure the fertile lemma awn separately (~0.3–1.5 mm). Confirm crowded whorls of ~10–20 short racemes, typically 2–5 cm.

Look first for widely separated panicle whorls with long racemes (~5–15 cm), often with one terminal upright branch. Then dissect a mature spikelet: measure the fertile lemma awn (~4.8–9 mm) and sterile lemma awn (~3.2–7 mm) separately.

Start with the annual basal crown, then the terminal inflorescence with roughly 4–20 digitate racemes mainly in one whorl. Dissect a mature spikelet: the fertile lemma has long apical marginal hairs (>1.5 mm) and an awn usually about 2.5–15 mm.
Inspect wiry branching stems with very narrow leaves and small yellow all-ray flower heads; basal foliage can be lobed.

On a bushy, sometimes sprawling plant with opposite triangular, 3-veined toothed leaves, inspect ONE flowering head from its side: it has a longer cylindrical involucre about 8–10 mm, with multiple (typically 4–6+) imbricate phyllary series. Contrast shorter hemispheric Conoclinium heads and white Ageratina shrubby mistflower; common name

Crush-free visual ID starts with the tiny narrow leaves: damianita is a low woody-based subshrub with many very narrow aromatic gland-dotted leaves and solitary bright-yellow heads held above the canopy on slender peduncles.

Look for a low, densely hairy plant with dark maroon-to-brown star-shaped flowers, commonly paired close to the stem and heart-shaped leaves. Then inspect the milkweed gynostegium in the flower center.

Look BELOW EACH HEAD for a second, obvious ARMOR COLLAR: a ring of spiny-margined leaflike bracts about as long as the 30–50 mm involucre. Those are separate SUBTENDING BRACTS, not the individual phyllaries of the involucre. Leaves often bear stout main marginal spines (5–30 mm, variable by variety) and cauline leaf bases may be auriculat

Start with woolly gray stems/leaves AND side of unopened head. C. ochrocentrum has strong, often straw-yellow phyllary spines (FNA large-headed keyed forms ~5–12 mm, other forms longer), while several middle/upper leaves may extend onto the stem as SPINY WINGS up to ~5 cm. Check glutinous/resinous midribs on outer/middle phyllaries if vis

FIRST measure the green involucre UNDER the flower heads (excluding florets and projecting phyllary spines): local Texas thistle specimen descriptions give roughly 15–20 mm in height. SECOND examine a stem LEAF NODE: the broad sessile upper leaf may make small spine-tipped clasping ears (auricles) and CAN continue as DECURRENT, SPINY STEM

Inspect full MID-STEM leaf shape and its TWO surfaces, then the SIDE of the involucre. C. undulatum tends to have gray-white wool beneath and relatively broader ovate/lanceolate stem leaves that are entire, coarse-toothed or shallowly lobed (not necessarily deeply feather-cut). In larger heads the involucre is often >3 cm; inspect a resin

Inspect the UPPER (adaxial) surface of a mature leaf with a hand lens. Bull thistle has numerous short appressed BRISTLELIKE SPINES projecting from the BLADE, not only spines at the margins. Also check the strongly decurrent leaf bases forming long spiny stem wings. This combination is more secure than purple heads, overall spines or wing
Start with the thick 3-parted to trifoliolate leaves and stout reddish stems, then confirm the unbranched tendrils and dark berry clusters.

FIRST find the slender open starburst of four pale SEPALS (no true petals) and numerous exposed stamens; purple/scarlet leatherflowers instead hang as leathery urns. Notice opposite compound often deeply LOBED leaflets and a twisting LEAF STALK that clasps supports. Male and female flowers occur on separate vines; only female vines produc
Look for the nodding leathery urn: dull blue-purple to reddish-purple sepals stay connivent for most of their length, then develop narrow expanded, often crisped/recurved tips.

OPEN masses of WHITE flowers on a climbing vine? Check the leafy stem and flower cluster. Sweet autumn clematis has MANY small white mostly BISEXUAL blooms in branching sprays, and opposite compound leaves with usually 3–5 oval, mostly smooth-edged ENTIRE leaflets.
