Look for the true scarlet leatherflower: a nodding ovoid-to-urn-shaped flower with thick rose-red to scarlet sepals and sharply recurved tips, but without the expanded crispate margins of C. pitcheri.
Beware stinging hairs; examine lobed leaves and white flowers without touching the plant.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Examine the very large, almost round leathery leaves with conspicuous reddish veins and the papery ocrea encircling twig nodes. Long hanging clusters of grape-like fruits help confirm the species; the fruits are not true grapes.
Look for alternate leaves with prominent veins from near the blade base, short axillary flowers and a small capsule; compare bud and twig details.

Find the green bract beneath the flowers: in Commelina erecta it is folded into a pocket, with basal margins joined and the top open for flowers to emerge. Then check the flower macro: smooth filaments and three fertile stamens plus three yellow staminodes, rather than Tinantia's six fertile stamens and conspicuous filament beards. Two bi
Woody shrub or small tree with stiff branchlets, small leaves and dark drupes; examine branching, armature and fruits against related Condalia and Ziziphus.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check for a smooth green stem with irregular purple blotches, then finely divided leaves and compound umbels of tiny white flowers. Confirm several structures together rather than relying on stem color alone.

Check a mature middle leaf: triangular/deltate to ovate with a continuous margin bearing teeth but NOT deep lobes or dissections; opposite leaves and blue-violet rayless heads support Conoclinium. Compare C. dissectum's palmately cut foliage.

Check fully expanded middle leaves: deep lobes or dissections interrupt the leaf outline; opposite foliage and blue-violet rayless heads support Conoclinium. C. coelestinum has a simple toothed—not deeply cut—leaf outline.
Leafless mycoheterotrophic orchid with thin pale to reddish stems and small orchid flowers; examine labellum patterns and floral spurs.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Find a large white, trumpet-shaped flower with a yellow throat; then inspect the broad, alternate, slightly rough-textured leaves and the persistent cup-shaped calyx around the developing fruit.
Start with the perennial clump and leaves: mostly basal/lower lanceolate leaves, long nearly leafless peduncles, and large all-yellow heads.

Start with life cycle, foliage, and ray pattern. Rock tickseed is an annual with narrow linear leaves and slender branching stems; the yellow ray florets usually carry rusty-red/brown color at the base.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check opposite simple leaves with several strong veins arching toward the tip. Feel the conspicuously rough upper leaf surface and inspect hairs beneath; when fruiting, look for clusters of white drupes carried on reddish stalks. The staged fruit photograph shows white fruit and reddish pedicels, not the diagnostic leaf h

Inspect the spurred yellow flower from the side, then compare mature capsules and seeds with C. micrantha. Golden corydalis typically has 13–16 mm flowers, and its fruits may spread or hang and curve; seed margin and fruit position depend on subspecies, so neither alone is decisive.

Look for the small spurred yellow flowers, then check for erect, often straight capsules and inconspicuous self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flower clusters. Measure mature seeds and inspect the margin; do not rely on raceme height or capsule length alone because subspecies vary.
Inspect grooved tubercles, areole spine patterns, flowers and mature fruit.
Low rounded cactus with pronounced tubercles and spiny areoles; inspect grooves on tubercles and flower position.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check for simple, alternate, broadly obovate leaves (widest beyond the middle) with mostly entire margins and a rounded tip. In flower or fruit season, seek large loose panicles with many fine elongated hairy stalks that create the characteristic smoke-like effect. The staged photograph shows foliage, not a diagnostic flo

EXAMINE FOUR THINGS IN THIS ORDER: (1) alternate simple leaves 4–7 cm, often 1–4 LOBES on each side and strong teeth; (2) woolly/white-hairy NEW twigs and flower cups; (3) 20 stamens whose ANTHERS are ROSE–PURPLE (not cream) in open white flower; (4) red pome 9–14 mm usually, 4–5 hard stones. Thorns may be present or absent, so never key
Inspect alternately arranged toothed leaves, thorny twigs, five-petaled white flowers and red pome fruits; verify against similar hawthorns.

For true C. capitatus, inspect the pistillate sepals and leaf tips: long pistillate sepals tend to spread or recurve outward after anthesis, and at least some leaves may be blunt or mucronate rather than consistently acute.
Start with growth form and leaf margin: this is a woody/subshrubby Croton, with ovate to ovate-lanceolate leaves and fine serrulation rather than an entire margin.
Look for ochraceous yellow-brown pubescence on young growth, consistently acute leaf tips, and pistillate sepal tips that remain straight to slightly incurved rather than flaring outward.

Start with the low branching habit and the pistillate flower. This is a small annual often branching from the base; the lower leaf surface lacks the brown-dot effect of Croton monanthogynus, and three bifid styles give six terminal segments.
Dark-centered stellate hairs create a brown-dotted leaf underside; two deeply bifid styles give four terminal branches, and the fruit is effectively one-seeded.
Separate male and female plants, narrow leaves, unisexual inflorescences, and a distinctly warty capsule.
Small hairy annual with narrow leaves and tiny white flowers in curled branches; examine calyx hairs and mature nutlets for species recognition.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Find the rough triangular to broadly ovate leaf blades, usually unlobed or only shallowly lobed, on a long trailing vine. Look for small round, often striped young gourds. This is a perennial from a substantial tuberous rootstock; do not excavate plants merely to verify it. The staged photo shows the leaves, vines and str

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check an annual coarse squash vine or bush with alternate often deeply 5–7-lobed rough leaves. At stem nodes inspect stiff hairs and their swollen pustulate bases; on a mature fruit look for a firm, five-ribbed stalk. The staged image shows a cultivated straightneck squash plant, flowers and lobed leaves, NOT a stem-hair
Find leafless twining parasitic orange or yellow strands on a host plant; inspect clusters of minute flowers, calyces and capsules.
Find the slender yellow-orange threadlike parasitic stems wrapped around a host plant, then examine tiny five-parted flowers and capsules for species ID.
Slender finely dissected ferny leaves and very small white flowers in compound umbels; look closely at the tiny ribbed two-part fruits.
Inspect cylindrical segmented joints, spines and tubercles, flowers and yellow fruit.
Pencil-thin jointed cylindrical branches, scattered spine clusters, and small scarlet ripe fruit.

Find the FLOWER CLUSTER where it meets an opposite-leaf node. Talayote has MANY very small (~5 mm wide) pale yellow-green flowers with WHITISH petal margins on a branching/racemelike AXILLARY cyme; larger Matelea milkvines have much showier netted or longitudinally striped flowers. An older plump smooth green follicle (7.5–9.5 cm long) an
Creeping stolons that root at nodes, narrow short leaves and several finger-like terminal flowering spikes; examine hairy ligule.
Inspect softly hairy, elongated leaves, coiled flower branches, and the prickly, four-part fruit that catches on clothing.
Look for terminal clusters of flattened spikelets subtended by bracts; examine glumes and achenes for confirmation.

LOOK FIRST underground: trace a full stolon from shoot to tuber. Softer/spongier stolons and commonly 6–11 mm tubers support yellow nutsedge; compare several mature persistent floral scales (~1.8–2.7 mm), often yellowish brown. Do not ID by yellow head alone.
Inspect the triangular sedge stems and umbrella-like clusters of flattened spikelets subtended by leaflike bracts; use mature achenes for confirmation.

LOOK FIRST at a FULLY MATURE spikelet: C. odoratus is unusual because a corky, winged spikelet RACHILLA disarticulates into one-fruited segments (each includes a scale, rachilla internode and achene). Usually subcylindrical spikelets; brown head color is secondary, not diagnostic.
Inspect triangular stems, the terminal umbrella of flattened spikelets and their leaflike bracts; check mature achenes.

LOOK FIRST underground: tough/wiry stolons and usually small (~3–8 mm) tubers distinguish purple nutsedge in combination with persistent, often purplish/red-brown ~2.6–3.4 mm scales. Don't rely on reddish seedhead color by itself.

LOOK FIRST at mature spikelets and the culm base: spikelets usually FLATTENED with relatively long DECIDUOUS floral scales, typically 3.2–4.5 mm, and a cormlike thickened culm base. Contrast odoratus mature corky rachilla that breaks into one-fruited units.
Look at texture before color: this is an herbaceous perennial with conspicuously silky few-foliolate leaves and a densely white-villous, fuzzy conic-to-cylindrical flower head.
Look for a perennial prairie clover with dense white cylindrical flower spikes and odd-pinnate leaves bearing several narrow leaflets; stems and foliage are conspicuously gland-dotted.
Look for narrow linear leaflets plus a dense swollen cylindrical-to-ovoid head. If the real question is D. compacta versus D. purpurea, move immediately to the calyx.
Look at spacing along the spike: flowers and broad bracts are visibly separated along a long slender, often nodding or drooping rachis rather than packed into a dense head.
First decide whether the plant is woody: black dalea is a low intricately branched shrub with many tiny leaflets on pale gray/straw branchlets and short terminal flower spikes.
Think low spreading grayish subshrub: stems can root at the nodes, leaves carry many small silky leaflets, and flowers are purple-violet.

Start with the leaves and flower spikes. Hall's prairie clover is a slender perennial with mostly 3-foliolate leaves, sparse wiry stems, and relatively loose spikes of conspicuous yellow flowers. The calyx ribs/teeth are often reddish-brown and hairy.
Look for compact white flower globes on a low, many-stemmed, gland-dotted prairie clover with mostly 3 narrow leaflets.
Think tiny yellow-to-purple Dalea: a very low perennial with silky compound leaves and ovoid flower spikes whose yellow flowers age rose-purple.
Look for a dry-country perennial prairie clover with pinnate leaves, noticeably downy foliage, and compact purple-violet flower spikes; mature calyx and leaflet characters help confirm it.

Start at the flower head, then move straight to the calyx. Purple prairie clover forms dense thimble-like to cylindrical heads; for the difficult D. purpurea versus D. compacta split, use calyx pubescence rather than flower color.
Look for the very fine-textured Dalea: leaves are consistently 3-foliolate with extremely narrow linear leaflets, and terminal flower clusters form small pink-purple globes.
Dense basal rosette of stiff narrow strap leaves with repeated small marginal teeth, producing a towering flower stalk of tiny cream flowers.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Look for broad, softly hairy gray-green leaves and large upright trumpet-shaped flowers. Inspect the calyx and the rounded prickly seed capsule to distinguish it from other Datura species.
Large white funnel-shaped flowers, hairy lobed leaves and rounded spiny seed capsules; verify against other Datura.
Finely divided carrot-like leaves, compact compound umbels of tiny pale flowers and bristly seed fruits.
Look for deeply divided leaves and spurred flowers arranged on elongated racemes.
Evergreen limestone shrub or small tree with glossy pinnate leaves, dense hanging clusters of purple pea-flowers, and thick woody pods containing bright red seeds.
Feathery highly dissected leaves, four-petaled yellow flowers and long slender mustard seedpods.

A small decumbent to ascending sharp-pod bundleflower: find 4–6 pairs of pinnae on a COMPLETE bipinnate leaf with a tiny cup-like extrafloral nectary beside the lowest pinnae. Heads have about 6–16 flowers (local descriptions vary); bisexual flowers with 10 stamens. Look for elongated pointed mature pods about 30–50 mm long. Critical comp

Look at the mature pod cluster first: strongly sickle-curved, comparatively BROAD pods about 15–32 mm long × 4.5–7 mm wide. Heads commonly have 20–70 flowers. Upright to spreading robust stems can reach 20–150 cm.

Look for slender prostrate to suberect prairie plants with very NARROW or linear leaflets. Small heads often have 4–12 flowers; mature pods are long, nearly straight and slender (about 35–70 × 2–3 mm), unlike the wide sickle pods of D. illinoensis.

Feel with the eyes: low woody-based sprawling shoots with FINE VELVETY hairs. Leaves usually 3–7 pairs of pinnae. Compare flower heads (roughly 15–33 flowers) and confirm 10 stamens per flower instead of the 5 of Illinois/prairie bundleflowers.

Often spreading to ascending perennial/subshrub; bipinnate leaves and small whitish heads with NARROW mostly straighter pods (often 30–80 × 3–5 mm). Habit is variable; confirm species with a full leaf, gland, flower heads and mature pods. Do not mistake D. virgatus var. acuminatus for this accepted species.
Inspect leaves in groups of three leaflets, branched racemes of small pink pea flowers and jointed pods that break into flat segments.
Perennial legume with three-parted leaves and small pea-like flowers; inspect the number and outline of joined pod segments, leaf surfaces and stipules.
Look for nearly stalkless three-parted leaves and small clustered pea flowers; confirm by jointed one-seeded pod segments rather than leaf shape alone.
Look at the small woolly plant with tightly clustered composite heads; compare the branching head clusters and phyllaries with other Diaperia.
Find the tiny silvery hairy spring annual and its compact flower-head clusters; examine the bracts surrounding each head.
Look for a low creeping mat with small kidney-shaped leaves on long stalks, then inspect the tiny solitary flowers and developing fruits beneath the leaves.
Start at the nodes and inflorescence: a taller plant with conspicuously ridged stems, broader opposite leaves, and paired axillary condensed cymes subtended by broad obovate bracts.
Find the finger-like terminal racemes; inspect paired spikelets, their hairs and the grass ligule.
Inspect wiry stems, narrow leaves and widely separated, delicate racemes; check spikelet hairs and arrangement under magnification.
LOOK HERE FIRST: opposite narrow leaves, interpetiolar stipules, and four-lobed tubular flowers in the leaf axils.

1) Older trunks have unusually smooth pale gray peeling/mottled bark; 2) leaves are SMALL (often 1.5–3.5 cm), simple, alternate, usually obovate with rolled-under margins and short hairs beneath; 3) immature berries green, RIPE fruits dark purple-black with persistent calyx. Never identify from black fruit alone.
Start with leaf size, bark, and ripe fruit: much larger leaves than Texas persimmon, dark blocky/checkered mature bark, and yellow-orange to reddish ripe fruit rather than black.
Inspect four yellow petals in a cross, basal deeply lobed leaves, and slender siliques (seedpods) on ascending stalks.
Start with the tiny low habit and very narrow opposite leaves. Then confirm solitary short-axillary lavender flowers rather than the paired bracted cymes of Dicliptera.
Check the dissected leaves, yellow composite flower heads and phyllaries; look closely at the disk florets and seed heads.
Ignore ray color first. Look for very narrow rough leaves and a usually single head on a stout little-branched stem, with drooping rays around a hard prickly cone.
Low ribbed cylinder cactus stems with densely patterned spine clusters; large pink-purple flowers.
Clumping cylindrical stems with long straw-colored spines and magenta-pink flowers; inspect spines and fruit.
Look for aquatic or wet-ground rosettes with long leaf stalks and three-petaled flowers in whorls; examine flattened achenes.
Opposite narrow leaves and tiny white composite heads; inspect involucral bracts and mature achenes.
Sandpapery alternate simple leaves; clusters of white flowers followed by fleshy yellow-orange fruit.
Inspect narrow silvery-scaled leaves, silvery twigs, small yellowish fragrant tubular flowers, and olive-like fruits.
Tiny tufted wet-ground sedge with narrow nearly leafless culms; inspect solitary terminal spikelet, dark scales and mature achenes.
Small tufted sedge with mostly leafless round stems, each topped by a solitary compact spikelet; inspect achene and bristle features.
Tufted wetland sedge with round leafless stems and one narrow spikelet per culm; confirm via tubercle, bristles and achene surfaces.
Wetland perennial with slender stems and one terminal spikelet; inspect stiff bent or rooting culms and the long-beaked achene tubercle.
Look for broad basal leaves and terminal clusters of small composite heads; inspect three-lobed florets and the surrounding phyllaries.
Pale flattened stem bases and several stiff fingerlike flowering spikes with tight spikelet rows.

LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect a mature, intact seed spike. Canada wildrye typically arches or nods with conspicuously long spreading/curved lemma awns. At a rachis node, check paired or sometimes three spikelets, then the narrow glumes with comparatively straight, V-like bases (not the strongly bowed, bony U-like bases typical of E. virginicus

LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect the base of the glumes on an intact mature spikelet. Virginia wildrye commonly has pale, hard, conspicuously bowed-out U-like glume bases; the terminal spike is usually erect and comparatively compact, with shorter straighter awns than Canada wildrye.
Look for a low, broomlike shrub of jointed green photosynthetic stems with leaves reduced to minute scales; examine seed cones.
Inspect the orchid flower lip and sepals, alternate leaves and moist-habitat growth; provisional recognition description.
Hollow jointed green stems with dark nodes and terminal conelike strobili; spore-bearing not flowering.
Annual habit + coarse many-flowered spikelets + crater-like glands on panicle branches, pedicels, glumes or lemma keels.
Look for hairiness before the airy panicle: conspicuously hirsute leaf sheaths plus distinctly bearded panicle branch axils are the strongest combination.

Start at the panicle and sheath collar. Plains lovegrass is a tufted perennial with an extremely open, airy panicle whose tiny spikelets sit on long divergent pedicels. Leaf sheaths are mostly glabrous, with hairs concentrated near the sheath apex/collar rather than being shaggy throughout.
Look for a tufted perennial lovegrass with very narrow, firm, inward-rolled leaves and a comparatively restrained panicle rather than the broad airy cloud of purple lovegrass.
Look for dense clusters of spikelets packed along the panicle branches. The spikelets often become violet to reddish, giving the inflorescence a heavier, chunkier look than purple lovegrass.
Look for the airy purple cloud. Purple lovegrass forms dense basal clumps but sends up a very open, flexible, widely spreading purple panicle that can break loose and tumble when mature.
Long hairs at the sheath throat/collar + glabrous culm nodes + a huge diffuse fine-branched panicle on a tall perennial bunchgrass.

SEASONS: (1) Autumn/winter flat rosette of shallow-to-coarsely TOOTHED, oblanceolate leaves, sometimes with hairs on leaf margins; (2) spring/summer a single erect leafy stem with very narrow ALTERNATE sessile leaves getting smaller upward; (3) terminal tall branching cone/panicle of dozens–hundreds of TINY ~3–4 mm capitula whose WHITE ra
Inspect the annual slender taproot, then compare lower spreading or deflexed stem hairs with straighter appressed hairs above.
Check for a thick woody root crown and persistent previous-year basal stems, then inspect phyllaries and rays.
Check numerous thin pinkish-white rays around yellow discs, hairy stems, and upper leaves that partly clasp the stem.
Look for narrow mostly untoothed leaves, stiff appressed stem hairs, and daisy heads with numerous fine white rays; compare the upper leaf bases.
Examine the silky flower branches and spikelets; look for the cup-like collar at each spikelet base.
Start with long narrow leaves and branched flowering stems; examine clustered tiny flowers and surrounding involucres.
A small tufted grass; examine the hairy spikelets, inflorescence branches and ligule to distinguish it from related shortgrasses.

LOOK HERE FIRST: inspect the finely divided, pinnate leaves and small five-petaled pink flowers. In fruit, look for the unmistakable long narrow storksbill beaks radiating from a cluster; the mature awns can twist into coils. Do not confuse this finely divided-leaf species with the broad heart-shaped leaves of Erodium texanum.
Low spreading plant with rounded heart-shaped leaves, magenta-pink five-petal flowers and elongated beaked fruit.

Start with color and leaf shape. Leavenworth's eryngo is an annual that turns dramatically purple in the flowering canopy; its upper leaves are broad, deeply palmately divided, and sharply spiny. The flowering heads are elongated and topped by a conspicuous crown of spiny bracts.

Start with the leaves: long stiff yucca-like linear leaves with spiny margins, topped by pale greenish-white globose heads. It lacks the vivid purple canopy and broad divided leaves of E. leavenworthii.
Trifoliolate leaves and bright red long tubular flowers on upright racemes; pods with glossy red seeds.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Inspect the four broad petals, finely dissected bluish leaves, caplike fused sepals on unopened buds, and long narrow seed capsules.

Differentiate late boneset from white mistflower/white snakeroot by its tall branched HERBACEOUS form, narrower opposite lanceolate gland-dotted leaves (usually 20–90+ × 5–40 mm), and 9–15 florets per capitulum. FNA describes 8–12 phyllaries in 1–2 series, each usually 1–3 mm long.

Start with the silhouette: E. angusta is an erect perennial from a thickened rootstock, not a low sandmat. Distal leaves become strikingly linear to elliptic-linear—more than 6× as long as wide—and stems/leaves are usually short-strigose. Confirm with the strigose capsule and white 4-angled seed with low transverse ridges or wrinkles.

First inspect the UPPER surface of an upper leaf or white-margined bract. If it is conspicuously hairy, then check bract shape: snow-on-the-prairie has long, narrow linear to narrowly oblanceolate white-margined bracts. The white display is bract tissue, not petals.

Start at the upper bracts: they are usually green with a sharply contrasting white, pink, or red base. Then inspect a cyathium: E. cyathophora has a single yellow-green gland that is sessile to substipitate, with an oblong opening and NO annular rim. Confirm with the glabrous capsule.

Against Euphorbia dentata, ignore overall habit first and go straight to the underside leaf hairs, then fruit and mature seed. E. davidii has shorter, stiffer, strongly tapered hairs often arising from minute pustular bases, larger capsules, and larger angular seeds with irregular low tubercles.

Against Euphorbia davidii, start under the leaf rather than at the overall habit. E. dentata has longer, weak, filiform hairs on the abaxial surface; then confirm the smaller glabrous capsule and the smaller ovoid seed that is rounded in cross section and evenly minute-tuberculate.
Look for branching herbaceous stems and the tiny clustered cyathia; inspect their cup-shaped involucres, glands and three-lobed capsules.

Think low perennial, not tiny annual mat. E. fendleri arises in dense clusters from a woody, thickened taproot/crown and has glabrous stems, small entire rounded leaves, and distinct narrow-linear stipules. Confirm with the glabrous depressed-globose capsule and relatively large white 4-angled seed.

Ignore leaf shape at first. Check the upper bracts and then the cyathial gland: E. heterophylla usually has green or only paler-green bracts and a yellow-green gland on a distinct stalk, with a round opening surrounded by an annular rim.
Look for opposite leaves on branching stems, milky sap and extremely small cyathia; examine the cyathial glands and three-lobed capsules.
Start at the flat creeping mat and opposite small leaves, often dark-blotched; examine milky sap, stem hairs and tiny cup-shaped cyathia.

Start with the UPPER surfaces of the upper leaves and white-margined bracts. Snow-on-the-mountain is usually mostly glabrous above and has broader elliptic to obovate white-margined bracts; then confirm with its hairy ovary/capsule. The white display is bract tissue, not petals.

Start with habit: E. nutans is an ascending to erect annual with arching branch tips, not a tight sandmat. Then check the relatively large opposite oblong leaves: the bases are strongly asymmetric, margins serrulate, and a reddish central blotch is common but not mandatory. Confirm with the glabrous capsule and finely wrinkled seed.

Start at a stem node. E. prostrata lies prostrate to decumbent but does not root at the nodes in the local Williamson County treatment; the upper-side stipules are free while the lower-side pair is fused across the node. Then confirm with fruit and seed: capsule hairs concentrate along the keels/toward the base, and mature seeds are sharp

Start at a stem node: E. serpens is the rooted mat in this trio. Its strictly prostrate glabrous stems frequently produce adventitious roots at nodes, often 1–2 per node in the local Williamson County treatment. At the same node, the stipules are fused into conspicuous broad-deltate membranous scales. Then confirm with a glabrous capsule
Find small cyathia among the leaves, then check cyathial glands and the three-lobed capsules under magnification.

Start with architecture, not the common name. E. villifera is usually erect to ascending rather than a rooted creeping mat. At the nodes its stipules are distinct and filiform, and the stem/leaf surfaces are papillate. Hairiness is supporting evidence only because glabrous forms occur. Confirm with the glabrous capsule, whose cocci are of
Small herb with tiny flowers and narrow foliage; check inflorescence form and fruit structures.
Low trailing or ascending herb with silky silver hairs and small funnel-shaped flowers; inspect leaf pubescence, calyx and pedicel.
Woody legume with alternate pinnate leaves of many small leaflets and slender white flower spikes; inspect leaflet arrangement and pods.
Shrub with opposite leathery oval leaves, silvery hairy undersides and flowers with fleshy white-pink petals and conspicuous red stamens; check fruit shape.
Inspect narrow sedge spikelets and stem hairs; check the style and ripe achenes under magnification.
Smooth green young branches and very large palmately lobed leaves; look for open boat-shaped fruit follicles carrying exposed seeds.

Check a fully opened FLOWERING SHOOT and an OPPOSITE mature leaf: this is a lax/sprawling herb with paired triangular-to-heart-based COARSELY TOOTHED leaves on long petioles and loose sprays of relatively small pale-pink/purple discoid heads. To separate fragrant mistflower (Chromolaena odorata), view ONE flower head FROM THE SIDE: Fleisc

Start with the tiny linear leaves. Narrowleaf elbowbush is densely twiggy with stiff 90-degree branching and very narrow leathery, often slightly rolled leaves. That skeletal, almost olive-like foliage separates it quickly from the broader-leaved F. pubescens.

Start with the leaves. Forestiera pubescens has noticeably broader elliptic to ovate leaves with some pubescence, and it is winter-deciduous. The rigid paired side branches still make the classic 'elbow' architecture.
Numerous tall thin spiny canes, temporary small leaves after rain, red tubular flowers at tips.
Identify an alternate-leaved shrub with prominent curved leaf veins; check buds, leaf margins and berries.

Once you know it is an ash, go to the lower leaflet surface and the samara: Texas ash usually has a glaucous white-reticulate waxy underside, a relatively small seed body, and a wing that is terminal or only slightly decurrent.

Count the leaflets and inspect a samara. Mexican ash usually has 3–5 leaflets with coarse sharp serration toward the tips; samara wings expand gradually from near the base, and occasional 3-winged fruits can occur.
Start with habit and leaflet size: a xeric shrub or small tree with tiny leathery, often nearly evergreen leaflets—commonly only three per leaf.

Look at the samara first: green ash has a larger seed body with the wing decurrent well down the body before broadening; then confirm a broad shield-shaped leaf scar and usually non-glaucous lower leaflet surface.
Woolly pale flower spikes on slender branching stems, narrow opposite leaves and papery bracts; examine mature fruits.
Inspect brown spikelets and leaf sheaths; examine the bristles, scales and mature achenes.

FLATTEN A MATURE LEAF in view: leaf edge often WAVY/crisped and blade narrow TRIANGULAR, with heart-shaped base. Then inspect an OPEN FLOWER face: large (~20 mm across), brownish/orange to green, 5 broad spreading lobes; white-pink fleshy corona inside. Unlike climbing milkweed F. cynanchoides, flowers generally are larger and lack the ma

Look at an OPPOSITE HEART-BASED LEAF with generally FLAT (not wavy) margins, then follow its axil to a clustered UMBEL of little creamy to rosy pink star flowers with a GLOSSY WHITE five-part corona in the center. The flowers are relatively SMALL, with petals about 3–6 mm, unlike large brown/orange F. crispum corollas (~20mm across).
Leafy-stemmed blanketflower with hairy alternate leaves and highly variable yellow/orange-brown rays that may be reduced or nearly absent.
Start with ray color. Maroon blanketflower is an annual with leafy branching stems and heads carrying dark maroon-red to purple rays, usually without the bright yellow tips common in G. pulchella.

Start with the long naked flower stalk and perfume. Fragrant gaillardia is a taprooted perennial with a basal rosette, very long mostly leafless peduncles, fragrant heads, and rays that may be tiny or completely absent, leaving a pincushion-like purple-brown disk.
Check trifoliate gray-hairy leaves, pea flowers and developing pods; compare leaflet surfaces with other Galactia.
Look at trifoliate leaves, pea-shaped flowers and flat pods; compare hairs on the leaflets and calyx.
Clinging hooked hairs on weak square stems and whorled narrow leaves, with tiny greenish flowers and paired bristly burr fruits.
Slender annual bedstraw with narrow leaves arranged in apparent whorls and very small four-parted flowers; examine the mature paired fruits and hairs.
Look for narrow opposite leaves and five-petaled yellow flowers; check reproductive structures.
Gray-woolly leaf surfaces and clustered small pale purple-brown papery composite heads; examine flower head bracts.
Shrub with opposite leathery leaves and conspicuous dangling catkins; examine leaf undersides and sex-specific flowers.
Twining evergreen vine with opposite narrow glossy leaves and showy fragrant yellow funnel-shaped flowers.
Deeply palmately lobed leaves, small five-petaled pinkish flowers and slender pointed beaklike fruits.
Inspect palmately divided leaves and five-petaled flowers; confirm with beak-shaped seed capsules and mature fruits.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Inspect the small five-petaled white flowers with numerous stamens and pointed green sepals, then check divided basal leaves and later the bristly round fruit cluster of hooked styles.
Notice divided leaves and blue-violet tubular flowers; inspect corolla lobes, floral tube and stamens before comparing other gilias.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Single fan-shaped leaves with repeatedly FORKING (dichotomous) veins, often notched at tip; leaves cluster on short spur shoots. Female trees bear fleshy-coated naked seeds, not berries or drupes.

LOOK AT A MATURE LEAF: larger prairie verbena often has a fernlike outline with deeply once- or twice-divided blades and many narrow secondary lobes. Then compare terminal flower clusters and watch mature spikes elongate in fruit. Do not identify by pink-purple flower color alone.

LOOK AT A MATURE LEAF: low or pink mock vervain has small, broadly ovate-to-triangular leaves (ca. 12–27 mm) with 3–6 pairs of comparatively broad fan-shaped primary lobes, often with secondary notches. Then inspect the very small flowers and the terminal spike: even in FRUIT the spike axis scarcely elongates.
Pinnately or twice-pinnately compound leaves, long flat pods, and stout sometimes branching thorns on bark and twigs.
Look for a vigorous twining vine with large opposite cordate leaves, relatively large uniform olive-green star-shaped flowers, and a long smooth follicle with strong longitudinal angles.

Inspect the yellow flower head and sticky involucral bracts (phyllaries), then the stems: yellow ray florets surround a disk; many phyllary tips hook or curve back; stems are noticeably hairy/glandular. Check serrate leaves clasping the stem.

Inspect the resinous head, stem surface, and mature cypsela: yellow rays around a disk, serrate leaves clasping the stem, glabrous-to-nearly-glabrous gland-dotted stems, and a pappus with numerous bristles. Do not identify from yellow color alone.

Start with the head: curlytop gumweed is typically rayless, with only yellow disc florets surrounded by many narrow spreading to ascending resin-gland-tipped phyllaries. Vegetative parts are strongly gland-dotted and aromatic.
Small woody shrub with paired tiny oblong leaflets, violet-blue five-petaled flowers and small colored fruit capsules.

Start with an open, wispy annual, heads at several heights, and yellow RAY + DISC florets. For the dangerous Amphiachyris amoena lookalike, inspect SIDE/BACK of phyllaries for possible green nerve borders and especially the tiny DISC-pappus scales. Habit and flower color alone cannot confirm.
Shrubby composite with sticky, resinous vegetation and small yellow flower heads; examine leaves and head structure.

Start at the small annual taproot and opposite oval to elliptic leaves; then inspect the lower third of the 5-6 mm calyx tube for its distinctive swollen (saccate) side. Flowers have a 9-13 mm, noninflated pink corolla. Do not rely on color alone.
Look for square aromatic stems, pairs of small opposite leaves, and small two-lipped flowers at nodes; inspect the flower calyx.
Inspect very small opposite leaves on four-angled aromatic stems, then use the tubular calyx and small bilabiate flowers for identification.
Start with small opposite leaves and aromatic square stems; examine the hairy flower calyx and two-lipped corolla for comparison with other Hedeoma.

Check the stem before the flower head. Bitter sneezeweed is the B028 species with stems that are ridged but NOT winged. Then confirm the very narrow linear leaves and numerous small yellow heads. Variety-level support: var. amarum usually has yellow disc lobes, while var. badium has dark brown to purplish disc lobes.

First decide annual or perennial, then inspect the stem wings. Common/fall sneezeweed is the perennial in this batch, with stout strongly winged stems and much broader obovate-to-lanceolate leaves that are often toothed. Its flower heads are also substantially larger than bitterweed's tiny heads.

Start with the stem and head shape. Pretty sneezeweed is an annual with clearly winged stems—the narrow leaf bases run down the internode as green wings. Its distal leaves are narrow and entire, and the involucre/head is notably globose. This separates it from unwinged H. amarum and from the more ovoid/obconic H. quadridentatum.
Annual or biennial sneezeweed with winged stems and an unmistakably elongated ovoid-to-conical central disk surrounded by yellow rays.
Grayish fleshy leaves and curled flowering branches lined with tiny pale tubular flowers; inspect leaf surfaces and fruits.
Clump of narrow arching fibrous-edged leaves and tall open flowering stalks with tubular coral-red or pink flowers.

In flower, look for a single yellow star/salver-shaped flower emerging from linear aquatic foliage. Joey's close views add a striking second cue: paired plants can show mirror-image style/anther handedness.
Dense bristly flowering spikes with long twisted dark awns that tangle together; inspect leaf sheaths and spikelet pairs.

Look for alternate, hairy and often glandular leaves; frequently subclasping upper leaves; branching yellow ray-and-disk flower heads. Inspect side of heads for glandular phyllaries and the coarse hairs at their tips; scent alone is unreliable.
Recognize a low stolon-forming grass with short curled leaf blades; inspect the distinctive short terminal inflorescences and spikelets.
Ignore the old Panicum label and look at the runners: long wiry stolons with swollen woolly nodes root to make new plants, while narrow upright seedheads rise from the sod.
Check the compact barley-like terminal spike with long bristly awns, then inspect the three spikelets grouped at each rachis node.
Round umbrella-like peltate leaves borne on long stalks, with small pale flowers on distinctive umbel clusters.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Check the rounded peltate leaf blades and their centrally attached petioles. Look for tiny flowers or fruits in spaced whorls along a slender stalk.
Look for divided leaves and flower heads dominated by tubular disc florets; inspect phyllaries, leaf segments and head arrangement to avoid confusion with similar composites.
Inspect finely divided narrow leaves and clustered pale disk-only composite flower heads; look closely at the phyllaries.
Inspect opposite small leaves, woody branching stems and four-petaled yellow flowers; examine mature capsules.
Look for a climbing vine with tendrils and lobed leaves; examine small unisexual flowers and bright mature gourdlike fruits.
Ask whether the holly is deciduous. Possumhaw drops its leaves and often leaves dense red-orange drupes exposed along pale gray twigs in winter.
Look at the leaf immediately: American holly is the big-leaved evergreen tree, with thick dark-green leaves bearing prominent stiff spine-tipped teeth.
Look at leaf size and persistence: yaupon is the small-leaved evergreen holly—tiny leathery elliptic to obovate leaves with low rounded crenate teeth.
Inspect compound legume leaves, small pink-red pea flowers and seed pods; confirm leaflet numbers and pod hairs.

Look for a sprawling or twining vine with thickened storage roots and highly variable heart-shaped to deeply lobed leaves. Flowers, when present, are pale pink to lavender morning-glory funnels with a darker throat.
Tall slender flowering stem with finely divided leaves and narrow red tubular flowers; inspect the five lobes at the flower opening and exserted stamens.
Erect annual with large opposite lower leaves and numerous inconspicuous greenish flower heads along upper branches.
Cluster of slender smooth often leafless stems with small narrow leaves in season; small pinkish flowers and milky sap.

Start with the middle-sized fruit and leaflet count. Arizona walnut usually carries 9–15 broader leaflets and fruits about 2–3.5 cm across—larger than little walnut but far smaller than typical black walnut fruit.

Start with fruit size and leaflet narrowness. Little walnut is the smallest-fruited local walnut: fruits about 1.4–2.3 cm and nuts about 1.1–1.7 cm, with 17–25 narrow leaflets. It is usually a shrub or small tree rather than a massive canopy tree.

Start with the fruit: black walnut has by far the largest fruit in this trio, usually about 3.5–8 cm, and the nut surface between the deep grooves is coarsely warty. Mature trees can also become dramatically taller and heavier-trunked.
On adult foliage, inspect the tiny scale leaves for a darker raised, nearly circular to hemispheric resin gland. Then confirm with dark-blue glaucous seed cones and thin shredding bark.

If a female tree has cones, start there: eastern redcedar has small glaucous blue-black cones about 4.5–5 mm across, commonly with 1–2(–3) seeds. Then inspect an adult scale leaf: the resin gland is pit-like/depressed near the base rather than a raised rounded mid-blade gland. Ashe juniper usually has larger 6.5–9.6 mm cones with one seed
Aquatic or riparian colony-former with long narrow opposite leaves and long-peduncled axillary flower spikes; white flowers carry purple spotting on the lower lip.
Start with scale and hairs: a very low suffrutescent mound with conspicuously ciliate opposite leaves and paired axillary pale pink-purple tubular flowers.
Look for a sprawling plant with paired leaflets, yellow five-petaled flowers and a segmented fruit; examine fruit texture.
Inspect compound or partially bipinnate leaves, large yellow flower panicles and inflated three-sided papery fruit capsules.
Find an intricately branched shrub with narrow leaves and unusual pinkish-purple flowers; inspect modified petals and beaked woody fruit.
Look for low trailing stems, narrow leaves, distinctive reddish-purple irregular flowers and spiny fruits; verify flower architecture and fruit.
Low spreading annual legume with leaves of three small leaflets, inconspicuous pinkish pea flowers and flattened one-seeded pods.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Turn a middle leaf over and find the row of stiff prickles along the underside midrib. Inspect clasping auriculate leaf bases and small narrow yellow-flowered heads; milky sap on a fresh break.
LOOK HERE FIRST: Upper opposite round scalloped leaves clasp the square stem; lower leaves have stalks. Pink tubular two-lipped flowers cluster at upper nodes.

Ignore flower color at first. Check the woody shrub habit, opposite rough leaves, and stems: Texas lantana is a winter-deciduous, non-spinescent shrub with stiff-hairy/scabrous 4-sided young stems and coarse serrate leaves. Then inspect the flower-head bracts and confirm the axillary pedunculate head.
Small resinous paired leaflets, bright five-petaled yellow flowers and fuzzy pale seed capsules.
Wetland grass with very rough cutting leaf margins and an open panicle of flattened one-flowered spikelets resembling tiny rice grains.
Recognize finely bipinnate leaves and spherical golden flower heads; check leaflets and flattened bean pods.

Start with WOODY SHRUB + small silver/ash-gray fuzzy leaves (densely matted fine hairs) packed along the branches. Then locate ONE tubular, two-lipped, five-lobed lavender to purple flower emerging from a LEAF AXIL. Count four stamens in two length pairs when flower is accessible. The common name 'Texas sage' is NOT Salvia texana.
Begin with opposite, deeply dissected leaves and tiny axillary flowers; check the hairy stems and seed capsules.
Unbranched spike of small purple discoid heads; use stem surface, corm, and fruit to teach local var. punctata versus var. mucronata.

Inspect opposite, thick, glossy leaves 3–6 inches long: look for a distinct opaque 1–2 mm rim at the blade edge and 6–8 pairs of lateral veins. Confirm large terminal flower/fruit panicles and woody tree-like habit.

Find opposite, narrow elliptic to oblanceolate leaves on nearly horizontal, spreading branchlets. Check that blades taper strongly toward very short petioles (often 2.5 mm or less), with mostly hairless leaf blades. Flowers and fruits are nearly stalkless (sessile to subsessile), unlike the distinctly pedicelled clusters of Chinese privet

Inspect an opposite leaf pair on an unpruned shoot: blades are thin, usually 1–3 inches long, often hairy beneath along the midvein, with hairy petioles and young stems. Confirm short terminal and upper-axillary white flower panicles.
Small upright herb with narrow leaves and spurred two-lipped flowers; inspect spur and calyx.
Aromatic shrub with alternate simple leaves and clustered flowers; examine buds, leaf texture, and berries.
Look for yellow composite heads, leaf texture, and distinctive head bracts; compare flower-head details with similar yellow daisies.
Look for slender stems bearing narrow simple leaves and five-petaled yellow flowers; check sepals and the developing five-part capsule.
Inspect narrow leaves, delicate five-petaled flowers and capsule structures; provisional recognition description.
Look for narrow leaves and yellow tubular flowers with fringed lobes; inspect floral throat and nutlets.
Erect spikes of brilliant red two-lipped tubular flowers above alternate lanceolate leaves; inspect the elongated staminal tube.

Usually an arching shrub or scrambling vine. Start at a TERMINAL flowering shoot: pale 2-lipped relatively short flowers, usually 17–20 mm, with connate/perfoliate terminal floral bracts. A leaf pair fused beneath the inflorescence does NOT prove coral honeysuckle; both share it.

FOLLOW ONE FLOWER STALK BACK TO ITS NODE. In Japanese honeysuckle, flowers are paired, two at a time, arising from LEAF AXILS along the shoot rather than a terminal whorl. The strongly two-lipped flowers start pale white and may age yellow. The mature berries turn dark/black (the others red).

Find TERMINAL whorls of LONG narrow trumpet-shaped flowers, usually ~38–48 mm. The top pair of opposite leaves/bracts often FUSES into a round disk below the head. But this is also possible in white/Texas honeysuckle—measure the narrow elongated trumpet versus L. albiflora's short two-lipped flower.
Check four sharp stem wings created by sessile leaf bases running down the stem; alternate lanceolate leaves and 4 yellow petals with 8 stamens confirm.
Usually upright/ascending and hairy, with alternate lanceolate leaves and typically 5 yellow petals plus 10 stamens; confirm long hairy bumpy capsules.

Locate several stem nodes: leaves alternate, typically narrow and softly hairy on upright branched shoreline shoots. At flowering, see a showy four-petaled yellow corolla and the conspicuously long inferior ovary BELOW the sepals; usually eight stamens. Compare L. repens opposite nodes and tiny four-stamen flowers.

Both this species and Ludwigia repens have opposite leaves on creeping stems. Find an axillary flower: palustris has four green sepals and no yellow petals. Do not rely only on absent petals because repens may be apetalous or shed petals. Check the ovary/mature capsule: palustris typically has four longitudinal dark-green bands across its
Creeping or floating mat of alternate glossy broad leaves, with typically 5 showy yellow petals and 10 stamens.

Inspect opposite paired leaves along a creeping, node-rooting stem. Look for very small yellow petals (when present), but note they may be shed or naturally absent. Crucially, a mature capsule lacks the four dark-green longitudinal bands seen on L. palustris. Do not force submerged sterile specimens to species.
Palmately compound leaves with five or more narrow leaflets; blue pea-like flowers on an upright raceme with a pale or white banner spot. Inspect flower structure and seedpods.
Sparse narrow-leaved branching plant with ligulate flower heads and milky sap; inspect the involucral phyllaries and mature fruit.
Inspect climbing fern fronds with finely divided, lace-like pinnae and distinctive spore-bearing lobes on fertile leaflets.
Inspect small opposite oval leaves and solitary five-lobed flowers on slender axillary stalks, with round capsules after flowering; flower color varies.

Start at the TWIG, not the hedge apple: alternate simple glossy smooth-edged leaves, stout single sharp AXILLARY THORNS on many young shoots, and white sticky MILKY LATEX where a twig or leaf is already damaged. Only FEMALE trees may develop the giant knobbly green multiple fruit (which can be seedless without nearby male trees). MALE tre
Inspect round to shallowly lobed, scalloped leaves and the small pale flowers clustered at leaf axils; confirm the segmented disk-shaped fruit.

Look for the flower architecture: five red petals remain tightly furled rather than spreading flat, while the staminal column and style project conspicuously beyond them. Then confirm the stellate-hairy, cordate to shallowly 3-lobed leaves.
Inspect square woolly stems, opposite wrinkled grayish leaves, and tight white-flowered whorls.

Notice what is missing: there are no ray florets. Barbara's buttons makes a rounded button-like head of many tubular disc flowers. Then check the narrow leaves, hemispheric involucre, numerous paleae on the receptacle, and the persistent scale-like pappus on the cypselae.
Look for wetland fern leaves with four wedge-shaped leaflets like a clover; identify stalked beanlike sporocarps for confirmation.

Compare the flower directly with pearl milkvine: it is more bell-shaped, with mostly parallel longitudinal green lines that become netted only near the lobe tips/margins, and the inner corolla surface is visibly hairy.

Look at leaf SIZE and flower SHAPE together: a wiry desert twiner with very small 0.5–2 cm leaves and tiny bell-shaped flowers with short triangular (2–3 mm) corolla lobes. Confirm the five-ridged cup-shaped corona at magnification.
Look at the flower first: broad flat pale-green lobes are strongly netted with dark green lines, and the center has conspicuous silvery reflective anther appendages—the 'pearl.'
Look for twining stems, triangular to heart-shaped leaves, and tubular snapdragon-like flowers; check flower and leaf details before distinguishing related vines.
Check the low creeping mat, toothed opposite leaves and small yellow five-lobed flowers; inspect corolla throat and seed capsules.
Low perennial with white ray florets surrounding yellow disc florets; check leaf arrangement and phyllaries.
Inspect bipinnate leaves, toothed leaflets, violet flowers and persistent yellow drupes.
Inspect three-toothed leaflets and an elongate raceme of tiny white pea flowers; look for small pods developing along the raceme.
Inspect toothed leaflets in groups of three, narrow clusters of tiny yellow pea-flowers and the developing legume pods.
Check toothed leaves, small pinkish flowers, and five-angled capsule; examine staminal structures.
Delicate climbing vine with tendrils, tiny yellow five-petaled flowers, shallowly lobed leaves and small melon-like berries.
Inspect opposite narrow to variably shaped leaves, yellow flowers with a short tube and mature paired fruit; check floral lobes.
Check opposite slender leaves and relatively long tubular yellow flowers; inspect corolla lobes and developing capsule.
Look for rough adhesive leaves and stems, pale yellow flowers and dry capsules; examine foliage and floral parts.
Look for twining stems, opposite leaves, small five-part flowers and milkweed-family floral structures.
Woody catclaw mimosa with many pairs of pinnae, strongly hooked infrastipular prickles, pale pink to whitish flower heads, and pods constricted between seeds.
Grayish thorny shrub with relatively straight stems, scattered less-curved prickles, 1–2 pairs of pinnae, and fragrant pink globose flower heads.
Low sprawling sensitive-briar with twice-compound leaves that fold when touched and pink-lavender globose flower heads.
Low prostrate creeping perennial with touch-sensitive leaves, pink globose heads, and broad prickly pods that do not narrow strongly between seeds.
Dark-stemmed woody mimosa with strongly curved downward prickles, few pairs of pinnae, pale pink flower heads, and short red-brown pods.
Opposite petiolate leaves and clusters of narrow tubular pale flowers enclosed by green floral involucres; inspect dark ribbed anthocarps after blooming.
Inspect narrow opposite leaves, floral involucre, tubular flowers and anthocarps.
Inspect opposite leaves, clustered small pink flowers held in bract-like involucres and the dark, ribbed mature anthocarps.

Inspect the floral bracts and calyx teeth: lemon beebalm has conspicuous long bristle-like tips, especially on the calyx teeth. Confirm with the interrupted stack of flower whorls and usually purplish floral bracts.

Start with the classic bee-balm head: an aromatic perennial with opposite leaves and a dense rounded terminal head of pale lavender to pink bilabiate flowers rather than the tiered bracted whorls typical of M. citriodora and M. punctata.

Look for cream-to-yellow corollas densely spotted purple plus pale white/pink floral bracts that are pointed but not long-bristled. Then inspect the calyx mouth: typical M. punctata remains open and ciliate.
Shrub or small tree with alternate, variable leaves and mulberry fruits; inspect leaf margins and fruit to distinguish other mulberries.

Start with scale and the ligule. Lindheimer muhly is a large dense fountain-form bunchgrass, commonly around 1 m or more tall, with unusually long conspicuous membranous ligules and a tall feathery panicle. It dwarfs seep muhly and is completely unlike creeping nimblewill.
Provisional source-concept learner. The source name appears erroneous and likely points to Muhlenbergia dubia; keep visibly flagged until provenance is corrected.

Start with plant size and blade texture. Seep muhly is a compact upright bunchgrass, usually about 40–80 cm, with threadlike involute leaves and a delicate open panicle that often develops a reddish cast. It is much smaller than Lindheimer muhly but still truly tufted, unlike creeping nimblewill.

Forget the ornamental-muhly silhouette: nimblewill is low and weak. Look for decumbent much-branched stems that root at the lower nodes, short flat blades, and a narrow contracted panicle. That creeping/rooting habit separates it instantly from the two upright bunchgrasses.

Look for the low rhizomatous habit and very fine rolled leaves. Aparejo grass is a short perennial muhly with creeping scaly rhizomes, slender culms, filiform involute blades, and small narrow panicles that may remain partly enclosed by the upper sheath.

Think intermediate between Lindheimer muhly and seep muhly: a dense upright perennial bunchgrass with firm folded leaves and an open erect panicle, usually in rocky canyons and prairie openings where the parent ranges overlap.
Inspect whorls of finely feather-divided leaves around emergent aquatic stems; compare the aerial and submerged growth.
Bushy submerged watermilfoil with feather-like whorled leaves and emergent flowering shoots that transition to broader serrate bracts.
Inspect the shrub's multiple-compound leaves, white flowers in large sprays and clusters of persistent red berries.
Look for a cool-season, wispy bunchgrass with a loose panicle and single extremely long twisted awns. Each fertile floret carries one awn—not the three-awned fork of Aristida.

Check the broad tree crown and a whole bipinnate leaf with generally few primary pinna pairs. Thorny twigs and pale cylindrical flower spikes lead to long straw-colored mesquite pods, not yellow spherical flower balls.
Large circular leaves on stout stalks, large pale-yellow many-petaled flowers and flat-topped showerhead-shaped seed receptacles.
Slender grasslike foliage and vivid blue-to-purple six-tepaled iris flowers emerging from narrow leaflike spathes.
Look for sticky foliage and narrow tubular pale flowers; inspect calyx and fruit capsule.
Dense clump of long, narrow, fibrous strap leaves with rough margins and a branching stalk of tiny pale flowers; inspect leaf base, marginal teeth, and inflorescence.
Recognize the tuft of long narrow tough leaves; inspect leaf margins, flowering panicle and mature fruit.
Look for narrow basal leaves and umbels of white six-tepal flowers on naked stems; check flower stalks and bulb traits.
Treat this as the tall biennial evening-primrose comparison: a first-year basal rosette followed by an erect flowering stem with yellow 4-petaled evening-opening flowers and elongate capsules.

Start with the white-to-pink gaura-type flowers and limestone setting. Limestone gaura is a perennial from a woody rootstock, with narrow leaves and asymmetric 4-petaled flowers that open near sunset and fade dark pink to red.

Start with the foliage and bud shape. Berlandier's sundrops has very narrow linear leaves, a low spreading perennial/subshrub habit, bright yellow 4-petaled flowers, and distinctly 4-angled/square flower buds.
Look for the mismatch between plant size and flower size: a tall, densely velveteen annual carries a long crowded wand of extremely tiny flowers—only about 3 mm across.
Start with the tall airy gaura-like habit: a robust winter annual or sometimes biennial with white asymmetric 4-petaled flowers that fade pink, long floral tubes, and a long-exserted style.
Look for an aggressively rhizomatous, hairy perennial with small white-to-pink gaura flowers and mature fruits conspicuously swollen or bulging on the upper half.
Tall riverbank evening-primrose with very long floral tubes and large yellow four-petaled flowers.

Start with the cut or lobed leaves and nocturnal yellow flowers. Cutleaf evening primrose is a low annual or short-lived perennial with alternate leaves that range from toothed to deeply cut-lobed, and 4-petaled yellow flowers that open around sunset.

Recognize the tall airy perennial first: wiry arching flowering stems carry white-to-pink four-petaled flowers with the petals held mostly toward the upper side and long exserted stamens hanging/projecting below.
Large four-petaled yellow flowers, narrow leaves, and conspicuous long seed capsules; compare floral tube and fruit.
Look for the low spreading habit, huge yellow evening-opening flowers, and especially the very large winged fruits. It is a dry limestone-prairie plant, not a tall riverbank primrose.
Do not expect a classic big evening-primrose flower. This is a delicate gaura-type annual with small white flowers that fade pink, long-exserted stamens and style, and narrow hairy stems and leaves.
A small perennial with pink to rose-purple four-petaled flowers, often in moist or disturbed places.
Look for a low rhizomatous perennial forming spreading colonies, with wavy or toothed leaves and small white flowers that fade pink to red.

Start with the flower architecture: a large, open, radial four-petaled primrose—usually pink to white—with 8 stamens and a conspicuous 4-lobed cross/finger-like stigma on a spreading rhizomatous plant.
Think gray-hairy rhizomatous gaura: narrow foliage and stems are usually covered with appressed gray hairs, and the small pale flowers fade pink to scarlet.

Compare the flower and fruit together: this annual has a mostly glabrous flowering spike with white 12–19 mm four-petaled flowers, crimson anthers, and a short chunky nutlike fruit with four major lobes/ridges.
This one should jump out from ground level: a flat, essentially stemless rosette produces a large yellow four-petaled flower on an extraordinarily long, sharply 4-angled floral tube.

First examine mature pads and areoles together: blue-green to glaucous pads, often with conspicuous long pale spines, and a woody branching cactus habit. Compare pad-and-spine characters against strict identified material; bluish color by itself is not a diagnosis.

Find an areole before anything else. On the flattened green cladodes, each areole is a specialized short shoot that can carry hairs, glochids, permanent spines, flowers, or new pads. Then compare pad shape, spine/glochid pattern, yellow-to-orange flower, and beet-red berry.

Treat this first as a taxon-concept card rather than a finished local key. Confirm current O. gilvescens identity before using historical phaeacantha labels, and prioritize pads, spines, flower, and fruit together when later diagnostic material is added.

Compare the whole plant against Texas pricklypear before counting spines. O. macrorhiza is usually a low, sprawling grassland cactus with smaller pads close to the ground. Then check the areoles: relatively few permanent spines, often with the main spine strongly bent or deflexed near its base, plus orange-brown glochids.

Use the brown-spine/desert pricklypear concept cautiously: low to spreading pads, usually conspicuous brown-gray spines, yellow flowers often with reddish bases, and fleshy reddish-purple fruit. Confirm the modern taxon concept before trusting old Central Texas labels.

Look closely at the pad areoles: many dense rust-red to reddish-brown glochid clusters, with ordinary long rigid spines typically absent. Then check the whole branching pad habit; do not use pad color or the red dots alone.

Inspect stem hairs with a hand lens: numerous straight, forward-pointing, closely appressed NONSEPTATE hairs distinguish this from the spreading, partly septate hairs of O. stricta. Then check upright/ascending stems, usually 1–3 flowers per stalk, and mature capsules (often 12–20 mm).

Find the underground BULB and basal trifoliolate leaves: the flowering scapes are separate, LEAFLESS stalks. Compare the broad, deeply notched leaflets (usually 14–34 mm, notch reaching 1/4–4/5 leaflet length) and ABSENCE of oxalate lines by the notch with the smaller, shallowly notched O. violacea. Examine stem and node hairs with magnification: O. stricta often shows spreading hairs, including SEPTATE hairs at nodes, rather than the densely straight, forward-appressed NONSEPTATE hairs of O. dillenii. Check flower-cluster size and mature capsules only as supporting traits.

Confirm BULB-origin basal trifoliolate leaves and separate LEAFLESS flowering scapes. Examine the small, relatively shallow-notched leaflets (usually 8–15 mm, notch ~1/4–1/3 depth): OXALATE LINES along the notch margins help distinguish O. violacea from O. drummondii. Flower color is not a reliable separator.
Look for slender branching stems and small pink-to-lavender heads with narrow ray-like outer florets; examine mature leaves and involucral bracts to separate related palafoxias.
Look for hair plus chaos: witchgrass is an annual with conspicuously hairy sheaths/nodes and an enormous, extremely open many-branched panicle that can look like a tumbleweed.
Treat provenance as diagnostic context: a warm-season bunchgrass with a fine open fan-shaped panicle that can resemble switchgrass, but arising from a firm knotty base and introduced from Africa.
Look for a short blue-gray bunch: mostly basal stiff glaucous leaves and a relatively small open pyramidal panicle whose branches are stiff and ascending.
Look at the base/collar and then the seedhead: a tall warm-season rhizomatous clump with a broad airy pyramidal panicle and a conspicuously hairy ligule/collar zone.
Inspect hairy stems with lobed leaves and a rounded seed capsule capped by a radiating, disk-like stigma.
Inspect fine opposite leaves and tiny greenish flowers protected by papery bracts; magnify the crowded nodes.
Coarse grass with racemose spikelet branches; compare spikelets, sheaths and ligules.

Next check small bracts under an open flower: affinis has them, lutea lacks them. Affinis's green-yellow flower is generally >25 mm wide, with wavy, clubbed outer corona tips (>10

Locate the conspicuous FEATHERY/STICKY THREE-BRACT CAGE just below a flower or around a developing fruit. Then inspect downy stems/leaves, coarse lobing, and odor if safely handled. Compare mature fruit texture/color carefully with introduced scarletfruit P. lanuginosa. Don't ID the local/native-concept plant using any globally labeled P.

Start with 2 distinct PETIOLE nectar glands and BROAD sharply toothed/serrated 3(–5)-lobed leaf; compare smooth edged narrow 3–9-lobed P. tenuiloba. Then check large purplish flower with layered corona and a fat maypop 30–60 mm, much larger than the little dark berries of green-flowered relatives.

Introduced scarletfruit passionflower comparison (not confirmed native to your target counties). Look first for an actual RIPE FRUIT: usually smooth and vivid red in the documented P. lanuginosa concept, versus greenish/yellow-green fruit in the locally reviewed P. foetida concept. Inspect very large opposite heart-shaped leaves, pale lavender tubular flowers and brown woody egg-shaped seed capsules.
Showy bladderpod relative with relatively large yellow flowers; it belongs in Paysonia rather than Physaria under the modern split.

Start with the woody base and leaf texture. Rock penstemon is a low densely branched subshrub with thick dark-green leathery leaves that have coarse mucronate teeth. It grows from limestone cracks and carries red tubular flowers on short stalks.

Start with flower size and the leaf node. Prairie penstemon has enormous pale lavender-to-white flowers, usually about 35–55 mm long, and opposite serrate stem leaves that are sessile and often fused across the node. The calyx and inflorescence are glandular-hairy, and the throat is abruptly inflated.

Start with scale and habitat: small lavender-violet flowers on slender branched stems in wet alluvial or coastal-prairie settings; sharp calyx lobes and an orange-haired exserted staminode are key details.

Start with the glossy leaves and the narrower pink-to-red corolla. Hill Country penstemon is an erect perennial with opposite dark-green leaves; lower leaves are often toothed while upper leaves become smaller and more entire/connate. Flowers are usually about 25–35 mm, distinctly smaller than P. cobaea.
Inspect opposite, strongly toothed aromatic leaves on a square stem, and the small two-lipped flowers arranged in slender spikes.
Check the strongly coiled scorpioid flower clusters and small blue-violet flowers; watch the arrangement of stamens and hairy foliage.
Annual with opposite narrow leaves, five-lobed flowers and hairy calyx; note flower tube and calyx teeth.
Evergreen hemiparasite growing on woody branches, with opposite leathery leaves and white berries; inspect nodes, flowers and fruit.

Look at the leaf before the flower head. Frogfruit has opposite oblanceolate-to-elliptic leaves that are usually widest beyond the middle, with the teeth concentrated on the upper/distal half. Then confirm the creeping stems rooting at nodes and the dense cylindrical flower spike on a long axillary peduncle.
Look for small alternate leaves on fine branchlets and inconspicuous flowers or capsules borne near leaves; examine leaf and stem attachment.
Low annual bladderpod with dense yellow flower clusters, stellate-scaly hairs, and round to obovoid inflated capsules on spreading pedicels.
Densely hairy perennial bladderpod with several stems from the base, bright yellow flowers in tight clusters, and small globose to ellipsoid fruits.
Delicate upright-to-sprawling annual with yellow-orange flowers and round to ellipsoid inflated capsules on straight or slightly curved pedicels.
Slender yellow-flowered bladderpod distinguished by recurved fruiting structures and inflated capsules.
Yellow-flowered bladderpod whose upper leaves are notably sessile, helping separate it from more obviously petiolate relatives.
Start with the narrow opposite leaves and upright terminal spike of pink-lavender bilabiate flowers. Compare leaf width and habitat carefully against P. correllii and the broad P. virginiana complex.

Think tall wetland obedient-plant: a rhizomatous perennial often over 1 m tall, with opposite narrow leaves and a long spike of pink-purple bilabiate flowers in saturated stream-edge or drainage habitat.
Upright rhizomatous mint-family perennial with opposite toothed leaves and dense spikes of pink-lavender bilabiate flowers.
Tiny leafless parasitic flowers emerging directly from woody host stems; inspect flower attachment and structure, not host leaves.
Look for alternate pinnate leaves bearing multiple pointed leaflets, red-to-blue small drupes in clusters and smooth gray bark on young trunks.
Find a low basal rosette and narrow flowering spikes; examine capsules, their opening and reddish mature seeds.

Start with the bark and fruiting heads. American sycamore has dramatically exfoliating mottled bark that exposes chalky white to pale tan patches, huge alternate palmately lobed leaves, and round hanging fruiting balls made of many achenes.
Start with leaf arrangement and head type: alternate, resinous/gland-dotted, usually petiolate leaves below a rounded cluster of many tiny pink-purple heads with no ray florets.
Aromatic, leafy composite with clusters of pink-to-purple discoid flower heads; inspect leaves, heads and involucral bracts.
Dense soft fuzzy bottlebrush-like flower panicle, formed by numerous long awns on closely packed spikelets.

Look for BROAD, FLAT spoon/obovate fleshy leaves with round or slightly notched tips and inconspicuous hairs at successive axils. Mature fruits open with a HORIZONTAL detachable lid but have NO expanded encircling wing like P. umbraticola. P. pilosa has narrow, near-cylindrical leaves and conspicuous long white axillary hair tufts. Yellow

At the transverse lid/seam find a distinct thin papery circular WING roughly 0.5–1.5 mm wide, BELOW the opening line, wrapping completely around the green fruit. Look for a broad-leaved submerged pondweed with alternate two-ranked leaves and a persistent axillary stipule/prophyll, then confirm the emergent many-flowered spike.
Think thicket-forming plum: slender often thorny branchlets, narrow serrate leaves, white spring flowers before or with leaf-out, and red to yellow plum-like drupes.

Think evergreen cherry: a small evergreen tree with glossy leathery alternate leaves, short axillary racemes of small white flowers, black drupes, and a bitter-almond odor when fresh twigs are scratched.

Start with the bark and spur shoots. Mexican plum is a small deciduous tree with gray to orange-brown bark, alternate simple serrate leaves, and clusters of fragrant white flowers on short lateral spur shoots. Then confirm the Rosaceae hypanthium, many free stamens, single superior ovary, and a glaucous purple-gray drupe.

Start with growth form and the short flowering shoots: creek plum is a clonal, thicket-forming shrub with alternate simple serrate leaves, small white flower clusters on short shoots, and rounded single-stoned plum fruits. Check leaf-margin glands when present, but do not require them on older leaves because they can be shed.

Start with bark, racemes, and leaf glands. Black cherry has alternate finely serrate leaves, elongated racemes of white flowers followed by black drupes, and older bark breaking into dark scaly plates. Local Edwards Plateau plants are commonly the accepted var. eximia.
Glossy, alternate oval leaves with finely toothed edges; clusters of five-petaled white flowers and small rounded fruits.
Rounded lobes, light gray scaly bark, shallow unfringed acorn cups.

Start with several mature, NOT juvenile, bristle-tipped leaves. Then check terminal buds (small, scales distinctly ciliate toward tips) and the mature acorn: a relatively deep goblet/cup-shaped cup commonly enclosing 1/3–1/2 of the nut. Compare against Shumard oak's generally larger, shallower-cupped fruits.

Think glossy narrow red-oak-type foliage: Canby oak has dark glossy evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves with serrated to bristle-tipped margins and a distinctly horticultural landscape presence in Texas.

Start with mature acorn shape plus the scaly cup: Texas live oak often has a narrow, noticeably pointed/spindle-like nut ~20–30 mm long seated in a relatively deep funnel/goblet cup. Combine this with pale appressed-stellate leaf undersides and central Texas limestone habitat; leaf shape or evergreen habit alone is insufficient.

Start with several mature blue-green, glaucous leaves—not a single shade leaf. A broadly rounded or notched tip, pale papery/scaly bark, and a barrel-shaped nut whose ends can look flattened are the useful combination. If the plant is shrubby, compare the twig and cupule carefully with white shin oak.
Look at the deep acorn cup that almost encloses the nut; then examine rounded leaf lobes and pale hairy undersides.

Inspect fruit first when present: bur oak has a large nut buried deeply in a broad mossy cup with soft projecting scale tips forming a shaggy fringe. Without fruit, look for a broad fiddle-shaped leaf with VERY deep middle/proximal sinuses (a narrow waist), then much shallower distal lobes or teeth. Corky wings on some older twigs provide

Look at adult leaf tips with a loupe: 3–5 broad distal lobes should show small AWNS/bristles (red-oak-group trait). Then check the conspicuous tawny-hairy, often 5-angled terminal buds (5–10 mm), glossy mature upper leaves, and dark bark broken into blocks. Do not rely on a 'duck-foot' leaf alone.
Inspect large oval leaves with rounded chestnut-like teeth and dense grayish pubescence beneath; then check the large acorn seated in a shallow cup.

Start with several adult leaves: chinkapin oak has an elongated chestnut-like blade with many regularly spaced teeth, each served by a near-parallel lateral vein; its sharp/forward-pointing teeth have NO red-oak terminal bristle. Turn over the leaf for a pale, minute stellate-hairy surface, and confirm a moderately sized acorn in a NON-fr

Inspect several mature leaves from one branch: water oak commonly has a narrow wedge-shaped base and a broader, often shallowly three-lobed bristle-tipped apex. Confirm small second-year acorns in shallow cups.
Check the leaves first: willow oak has long, narrow, unlobed willow-like blades with smooth margins and a tiny terminal bristle. Then check the small acorns in shallow saucer-like cups.
Look for the mostly unlobed to shallowly toothed, leathery evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves. The acorn cup is deeper than in Shumard oak and may enclose roughly half the nut.

Start with the red-oak leaf architecture: large deciduous leaves with 5–9 deep bristle-tipped lobes and conspicuous tufts of hair in the vein axils beneath. Then confirm with the shallow saucer-shaped acorn cup covering only about one-quarter to one-third of the nut.

Use the whole plant first: a dry-limestone shrub or small multi-stemmed tree, commonly a low thicket. Then inspect bud, mature leaf underside, and ripe acorn cup—the cup scales are flattened, NOT strongly tuberculate. Leaf outline alone is unreliable.

Check multiple mature leaf lobe tips: usually rounded with NO terminal bristle. If the leaf lacks a clear cross-shaped outline, look at thick (2–5 mm), often yellowish, densely stellate-hairy twigs and the harsh/stippled LOWER leaf surface with crowded yellowish glandular hairs plus minute stellate hairs. Check leathery evergreen to subevergreen NARROW leaves with a few large teeth (or entire margins), then dark bark peeling in long strips. Confirm a tiny shallow cup with strongly, regularly BUMPY/tuberculate scales; this beats leaf shape by itself.
Compare leaf breadth, lower-surface pubescence, acorn shape, geography, and Q. fusiformis overlap. Ambiguous Central Texas live oaks should remain unresolved.
Early-flowering buttercup with divided basal foliage, several yellow glossy petals and rounded aggregates of small achenes.
Large yellow many-stamened flowers on herbaceous stems with lobed basal leaves; confirm petal size and mature achene head.
Inspect hairy stems and three-lobed lower leaves; small glossy yellow five-petaled flowers followed by a rounded head of achenes.
Moist-site herb with divided or lobed leaves, small yellow flowers and a long cylindrical cluster of many small achenes.
Observe small four-petaled yellow mustard flowers and distinctly two-parted fruit with a swollen upper segment; inspect leaves and fruiting stems.
Evergreen shrub with alternate leathery toothed leaves, terminal clusters of white-to-pink five-petaled flowers and small dark pomes.
Count leaflets first: fragrant sumac has exactly 3. The leaflets are often fan-shaped, lobed or coarsely toothed on a low suckering deciduous shrub.
Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.
Start with the tiny compound leaves: a thornless densely branched shrub with odd-pinnate leaves made of several very small dull-green leaflets, sometimes on a narrowly winged rachis.
Look for leathery evergreen foliage: alternate compound leaves usually have only 5–9 thick, smooth-edged leaflets that are glossy dark green above.
Twining stems, trifoliate leaves, yellow pea flowers and legumes.
Check the three leaflets, papilionaceous yellow flowers and small legumes; compare leaflet shapes and fruit traits with other Rhynchosia.
Inspect alternate leaves, five-petaled mallow flowers and inflated fruiting calyx.
Look for delicate branching stems, ovate leaves, small pale flowers in racemes and conspicuous red berries; check fruit arrangement.

LOOK HERE FIRST: Check the pinnately compound leaves with smooth-edged oval leaflets and the paired short stipular spines at twig nodes. In flower, look for drooping clusters of white pea-shaped blossoms; later look for flat pods.
